ID: UQ-20261016-13
Date: 2026-10-16
Status: Rejected
Domain(s): Medicine — clinical microbiology, antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) and breakpoint standard-setting; donor field: veterinary/aquaculture AST (CLSI VET03/VET04 species-appropriate incubation temperatures)

Question (canonical):
When a standard broth-microdilution panel is incubated at the measured temperature of the infection site rather than at the standard 35 ± 2 °C, what fraction of susceptible/intermediate/resistant calls flips, and does the flip rate concentrate in particular agent classes?

Alternative formulations:
1. (Gate 1 reformulation, the version judged) For a pre-specified isolate x agent panel (cool-site isolates — chronic wound, diabetic foot, burn eschar, CF airway — plus a bacteraemia set), tested by ISO 20776-1 broth microdilution in replicate at 35 °C and in parallel at 31/33 °C (cool arm) and 39.5 °C (febrile arm), with pre-specified reading rules and a reading-time-only control arm at 35 °C: what is the paired within-isolate S/I/R discordance rate versus the 35 °C arm under current EUCAST/CLSI breakpoints, does it exceed the same experiment's replicate discordance at 35 °C, and is the excess concentrated in identifiable agent classes?
2. Are EUCAST/CLSI breakpoints, all set at 35 ± 2 °C, transportable to cool-site infections (~31-34 °C) and to febrile bacteraemia (39-40 °C)?
3. Is the incubation temperature written into the AST standard a hidden determinant of reported resistance rates, in excess of the method's own reproducibility limit?

Motivating gap:
Aquatic-animal AST cannot assume one incubation temperature (CLSI VET03/VET04, ~22-28 °C) and has had to stratify ECV derivation by temperature; human clinical AST fixes 35 ± 2 °C and applies the resulting breakpoints to sites that are not at 35-37 °C. Gate 2 found the gap as stated to be largely false: human clinical microbiology asked this repeatedly in 1982-1996 and answered the febrile half at panel scale in 1982. The intake's "no own-field literature" note was a query artefact — dropping "infection-site temperature" and "breakpoint" and using the plain own-field title form surfaces the literature immediately.

Presuppositions:
1. Site temperatures at the named sites differ from 35 ± 2 °C enough to matter — partly established (wound-bed and airway-temperature literature), not quantified against a one-doubling-dilution threshold.
2. "The infection-site temperature" is an abstraction (spatially/temporally heterogeneous) — conceded at intake, handled by fixing discrete temperatures.
3. In-vitro incubation temperature is a defensible surrogate for the in-vivo thermal condition — CONTESTED (temperature also moves immune effectors, perfusion, local exposure); scoped to measurement-internal validity only.
4. Breakpoints are intended as site-transportable organism-drug properties — true as deployed, but PK/PD-derived breakpoints already embed site exposure assumptions, so the inversion is partial and agent-specific.
5. Growth at 31/33 °C is adequate for a readable panel in the standard window — CONTESTED; reading time is a confounder (hence the control arm).
6. Flip rates are comparable against essential agreement (one doubling dilution) — defensible; this comparator is the candidate's one genuine methodological addition.
7. (Gate 1) Holding the breakpoint fixed while moving the measurement condition is a meaningful operation; re-deriving breakpoints per temperature changes the question's shape.

What would count as an answer:
The paired within-isolate experiment above: a matrix of MIC shifts in doubling dilutions plus the S/I/R discordance rate versus 35 °C under current breakpoints, by agent class, with same-experiment 35 °C replicate discordance as comparator and the reading-time-only arm subtracted. "Hidden determinant" = discordance for one or more classes materially exceeds replicate discordance; "no" = all within the reproducibility bound, which would positively establish the transportability the standard assumes. Specifiable, finite, falsifiable — well-posedness is not where this candidate fails.

Novelty — queries run (query → one-line result):
11 queries (full list and per-query results: batches/2026-10-16-0433/UQ-20261016-13-record.md), 5 fetches, budget exhausted at the cap rather than at field exhaustion. Most informative:
- "influence of incubation temperature on antimicrobial susceptibility testing results broth microdilution MIC categorical agreement" → multiple on-point own-field hits, incl. a Galway record "Influence of incubation temperature and time on the precision of ..." and two records on effects of incubation temperature/inoculum/reading time on agar dilution and diffusion.
- "temperature-dependent antibiotic susceptibility MIC shift clinical breakpoint 35 °C infection site temperature" → PMID 7069235 (prior 1), PMC271193, PMC181849.
- "oxacillin resistance detection 30 °C versus 35 °C incubation temperature MRSA heteroresistance susceptibility category" → PMC271193 (prior 2, 2,397 isolates).
- "reduced incubation temperature 30 33 degrees minimum inhibitory concentration susceptibility category change clinical isolates antibiotic class" → jcp.bmj.com/content/38/9/1055 (prior 3) plus PMC185682, PMC499358.
- "why 35 °C incubation antimicrobial susceptibility testing standardization history CLSI breakpoint temperature chosen" → PMC6325273 on adherence to optimal incubation temperature for resistance monitoring (blocked by CAPTCHA, title only), and a 2019 SciTePress paper doing the exact 33-vs-35 °C gentamicin/S. aureus comparison.
- "commutability transportability of a diagnostic cut-off across measurement conditions matrix effect laboratory medicine antimicrobial breakpoint" → only generic commutability/CLSI EP14 material; this framing is genuinely absent from AST — a vocabulary gap, not a question gap.

Novelty — nearest prior formulations (3, with sources):
1. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7069235 (abstract read; bibliographic header did not render, so the attribution is unverified — content verified). MICs and serum bactericidal activity across the physiologic range, 17 agents x 432 strains, 35-41.5 °C; activity rose progressively with temperature; at 41.5 °C ~17% of MICs were >=4-fold lower than at 35 °C, 7% >=8-fold, 2% >=16-fold.
2. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC271193 — Welch & Southern, J Clin Microbiol 1984;19(6):831-833 (PMID 6565708). 2,397 S. aureus isolates, agar dilution at 30 vs 35 °C; methicillin MICs agreed for 93%, 6.8% discordant, 2.5% resistant at 30 °C and susceptible at 35 °C.
3. https://jcp.bmj.com/content/38/9/1055.long — Wheat, Winstanley & Spencer, "Effect of temperature on antimicrobial susceptibilities of Pseudomonas maltophilia", J Clin Pathol 1985;38(9):1055. 20 strains plus comparators, panel of agents, 30 vs 37 °C; significantly less susceptible at 30 °C for aminoglycosides and polymyxin B only.
Supporting: Rahmati-Bahram, Magee & Jackson, J Antimicrob Chemother 1996;37(4):665-676, doi 10.1093/jac/37.4.665 (citation verified, abstract not read) — mechanism for prior 3. Title-only and unopened, not relied on: PMC6325273; the Galway temperature-and-time precision record; SciTePress 2019 33-vs-35 °C gentamicin paper.

Novelty — how this differs from each:
vs prior 1: this is the candidate's febrile arm, already executed at panel scale over a wider excursion. Differences are design-level only — fold-shift distribution rather than S/I/R discordance under today's breakpoints, no replicate comparator, no cool arm, no cool-site sampling frame, no reading-time control.
vs prior 2: this is the candidate's headline quantity (cool-arm category-flip rate) at large scale for one organism-drug pair; 30 °C is used as an MRSA detection device rather than a site-temperature surrogate, so the motivation is inverted, and there is no reproducibility comparator.
vs prior 3: this is the "does it concentrate in agent classes?" sub-question, asked and answered affirmatively for one organism (aminoglycosides, polymyxin B). Differences: sampling frame, category rather than MIC reporting, no comparator, 30/37 vs 31/33/35 °C.
Net: a scaled-up, metrologically sharpened version of a question the field asked in 1982-1996 and partly answered. The only element with no prior found is the framing of a breakpoint as a cut-off whose transportability across measurement conditions is tested against the method's own reproducibility bound — a framing contribution, not an un-asked question.

Novelty confidence: Low

Significance — consequence:
A "yes" would turn the 35 ± 2 °C clause of ISO 20776-1 / CLSI M07 from a standardization convention into a reported determinant of the S/I/R label for a named population, forcing a choice between a cool-site reporting caveat, site-qualified breakpoints, or explicit documented acceptance; the S. maltophilia aminoglycoside history shows the committees do act at organism-drug granularity. A "no" is the more informative branch and the one the priors do not supply. Weakening both: prior 1's monotonic 35-41.5 °C result makes the febrile answer close to predictable from a 1982 abstract, so informative content is confined to the cool arm and the class-concentration pattern.

Significance — audience:
EUCAST Steering Committee / CLSI AST Subcommittee (they write the incubation clause and already issue organism-specific reporting suppressions); laboratories serving diabetic-foot, burn and CF services; CF and wound-care research groups arguing routine AST predicts outcome poorly; veterinary/aquaculture standard-setters wanting a human reference point. The audience is real; what is not supported is that it would be surprised — it has held partial cool-arm evidence since 1984 and the clause still reads 35 ± 2 °C.

Significance — fecundity:
Whether PK/PD breakpoint derivation needs a temperature term for cool-site targets; whether the same transportability test applies to the standard's other fixed clauses (pH, CO2, broth cation content, inoculum density) as a general "which clauses are classifier inputs" programme; whether flip rate predicts cool-site outcome; whether temperature-sensitive classes share an uptake-energetics mechanism predicting the class list a priori; whether surveillance rates for cool-site specimen types carry a correctable bias.

Significance — anchoring:
In-vitro/in-vivo discordance in AST (notably CF and chronic wound); the biofilm-versus-planktonic critique, of which this is the thermal analogue; ECV derivation in veterinary/aquaculture AST where temperature is already a stratifier; cut-off commutability across measurement conditions, which clinical chemistry frames and AST does not.

Reason for silence:
There is no silence to explain — the question was asked. The supported mechanism is answer attrition inside a standards regime: the 1982/1984/1985/1996 findings were absorbed as organism-drug caveats rather than as a challenge to the thermal clause, because the standard exists to deliver inter-laboratory comparability and site-specific incubation trades that for in-vivo fidelity the standard never claimed. Secondary: the 1984 cool-temperature data entered the literature under "MRSA detection sensitivity", so searchers using transportability vocabulary miss it — the same vocabulary trap that produced the intake's false gap.

Adversarial log (8 rows: attack | objection | response | status):
1. Triviality | not run | — | Not run (Gate 4 not reached)
2. Disguise | not run | — | Not run — UNVERIFIED (no adversary executed the required >=8 fresh-vocabulary Disguise queries; on this ground alone the entry could not have been Validated, and the generator's own Gate 2 note that any adversary accepting the question as un-asked should be treated as suspect stands untested)
3. Combinatorial novelty | not run | — | Not run
4. Presupposition failure | not run | — | Not run
5. Vagueness | not run | — | Not run
6. Significance inflation | not run | — | Not run
7. Reason for silence | not run | — | Not run
8. Dissolution | not run | — | Not run
Gate 4 was not run because the candidate failed Gate 2; no adversary file exists for this ID.

Scores: Well-posedness 3/3 · Significance 2/3

Strongest remaining objection:
The candidate is a disguised known. Every component is answered in its own literature within 11 queries: the febrile arm at panel scale (prior 1, 17 agents x 432 strains), the cool-arm category-flip rate at large isolate scale (prior 2), and the class-concentration sub-question affirmatively (prior 3, with mechanism in 1996). What is new is a comparator and a sampling frame — a better-designed study of an asked question, plus an unused metrological vocabulary. Rejected at Gate 2: novelty Low. Scoring well on well-posedness and significance cannot rescue it, and the untested Disguise attack can only have lowered novelty further, never raised it.

Suggested first step toward an answer (pointer only — do not take it):
Before anything else, open the three own-field records Gate 2 left unread — PMC6325273, the Galway "incubation temperature and time" precision study, and the 2019 SciTePress 33-vs-35 °C gentamicin paper — since any of them may close the narrow cool-arm residue below and remove the routing row.

Routing (if rejected as already-asked):
Routed. The febrile arm is asked and substantially answered and is NOT routed. The narrow cool-arm residue — a panel-level, multi-species S/I/R discordance rate at 31/33 vs 35 °C in cool-site isolates, referenced to same-experiment replicate discordance, with a reading-time control — is asked at organism-drug granularity and not answered at panel level; one row appended to ledger/routed-open-problems.md. Caveat carried into the row: given how dense the own-field prior art proved inside the query cap, the residue is not safely assumed un-asked, and the three unread records above must be checked before work starts.

The rejection does not depend on the attribution: what matters is that a panel-scale febrile-temperature MIC study on 432 strains exists at that PMID, and its content is verified twice over.

ID: UQ-20261016-14
Date: 2026-10-16
Status: Rejected
Domain(s): Medicine — clinical genetics and diagnostic laboratory practice (phasing); neighbours: lab quality assurance, screening epidemiology, pharmacogenomics, precision oncology

Question (canonical):
In a defined archive of issued diagnostic reports asserting an autosomal-recessive molecular diagnosis on two heterozygous variants in one gene whose phase was never established by trio testing or read-backed phasing, (a) what fraction of retrievable, re-phaseable cases have both variants on one haplotype under long-read phasing — with a CI, stratified by inter-variant distance, gene, report era, and whether a population cis/trans prior was cited — and (b) among those cis cases, what fraction have no alternative second allele after a pre-specified search for deep-intronic, structural and methylation events (the strict false-diagnosis fraction)? (V2, adopted at Gate 1; V1 intake wording and reason for reformulation in the record.)

Alternative formulations:
- Now that phase is directly observable at arbitrary variant separations, how many legacy "compound heterozygous" diagnoses were wrong because both variants sat on one haplotype?
- What is the positive predictive value of a recessive molecular diagnosis issued without phase information, stratified by inter-variant distance and by whether population cis/trans priors were invoked?

Motivating gap:
Phase is load-bearing for a recessive diagnosis (ACMG/AMP PM3 encodes trans as the evidential requirement) and was inferred, not observed, before long reads. Single-case long-read phasing demonstrations exist (WNT10B, PMC11973024); the field's two adjacent programmes run the other way — prospective population phase inference (Guo et al. 2024) and long-read reanalysis of UNSOLVED cases to raise yield (Smith et al., ASHG) — so, per the Gate 2 reading, nobody re-tests solved cases. Gate 4 overturned this premise.

Presuppositions:
1. A non-trivial share of issued recessive diagnoses had phase unresolved. Load-bearing; NOW SUPPORTED — 125/293 (~43%) of Guo et al.'s presumed-causal pairs were proband-only.
2. Stored DNA retrievable, consented, adequate for long-read phasing. Contested; selection hazard, handled in V2 by defining the estimand on the retrievable archive.
3. Long-read cis calls are not artifacts (switch error, dropout, segdup mismapping). Requires a stated error model plus orthogonal confirmation; error model unspecified.
4. A cis pair falsifies the diagnosis. Contested; split in V2 into "phase wrong" (primary) and "diagnosis wrong" (secondary).
5. Report text records how phase was established well enough to define the eligible subset. Untested; testable in-study.
6. Implicit: a cis finding is actionable (recontact, reissue). Jurisdiction- and consent-dependent.

What would count as an answer:
A retrospective re-phasing audit in one or more diagnostic labs: eligible subset coded from report text; retrievable DNA re-phased by long-read or targeted linked-read sequencing with a stated switch/dropout error model and orthogonal confirmation of cis calls; cis proportion with CI, stratified as above; share of cis cases with no alternative second allele; retrievability reported as a denominator against issued reports. "No" = cis fraction inside a pre-registered equivalence margin around the method's own error rate.

Novelty — queries run (query → one-line result):
Gate 2: 11 web searches in five vocabularies, 5 fetches (both caps reached) — full list and per-query results in batches/2026-10-16-0433/UQ-20261016-14-record.md. Most informative: "long-read sequencing resolves phase previously reported compound heterozygous variants ... diagnostic laboratory cohort" → single-case phasing only; "variants in cis misdiagnosis autosomal recessive apparent compound heterozygosity proportion" → Guo et al. 2024 (population inference); "retrospective long-read phasing candidate biallelic variants diagnostic cohort proportion in cis diagnosis revoked" → Cao et al. 2026 (somatic) and Smith et al. ASHG (lrWGS on unsolved cases); "long-read genome sequencing reanalysis of previously solved rare disease cases changed interpretation cohort percentage" → reanalysis literature measures diagnoses gained only. Guo et al. full text BLOCKED (PMC captcha) — recorded at the time as the single decisive blind spot.
Gate 4: 18 further searches, 8 fetches across two adversaries (batches/2026-10-16-0433/UQ-20261016-14-adversary-1.md, -adversary-2.md). Decisive: A2 query 4, German ("Phasenbestimmung compound-heterozygot 'in cis' Fehldiagnose Elterndiagnostik Anteil autosomal-rezessiv") → open bioRxiv full text of Guo et al. (10.1101/2023.03.19.533370), read in full; A2 query 5, Chinese → AlAbdi et al., "Diagnostic implications of pitfalls in causal variant identification based on 4577 molecularly characterized families" (Nat Commun 2023), an own-field audit of already-solved families with a variant-level-inheritance / "complex compound inheritance" pitfall class that Gate 2 never found; A1 query 2 → the ABCA4 "complex allele" locus-wide phase literature (PMC7479065, PMC8255130, PMC6947411, PMC8948157), A1 query 1 → alpha-globin cis/trans, i.e. the gene-level literatures Gate 2 flagged as risk (ii) and never searched.

1. vs Guo 2024: it does not differ enough. Guo's validation set is 627 Broad CMG patients with confident/strong recessive diagnoses — the candidate's own target population. That is the candidate's primary estimand, measured retrospectively on issued recessive diagnoses, with a denominator and with recontact. The residual differences — direct observation instead of inference, an issued-report rather than research-cohort denominator, era/prior-citation strata, and the second-allele adjudication — are a better-instrument re-measurement and an extra secondary outcome, not an un-asked question.

Significance — consequence:
If the cis fraction materially exceeds the method's error rate: phase-unknown becomes a hard bar or a mandatory-confirmation trigger; a recontact obligation falls on a definable subset of past reports; downstream recurrence risks (25% vs near-0), relative carrier testing, therapy and trial eligibility are re-examined. If inside an equivalence margin: licenses continued phase-free reporting in defined circumstances and redirects reanalysis capacity to second-allele discovery. Discounted at Gate 4: with a prior now in evidence of ~2-4% inferred cis, much of it at separations where read-backed phasing already applied, the promised movements shrink toward the margin.

Significance — audience:
Diagnostic lab directors and curation teams (hold archives and templates); ClinGen SVI and disease VCEPs (own PM3's wording and the CSPEC specifications — the real lever); CAP/ISO 15189/EMQN (checklists, a phase-resolution EQA challenge); clinical geneticists and counsellors quoting recurrence risk; payers and national programmes on long-read reimbursement; GREGoR/Genomics England. Audience reality is not in dispute — Guo et al. contacted the responsible clinicians over seven cis calls.

Significance — fecundity:
Calibrates the distance threshold past which prior-based phasing is unsafe; first direct estimate of the undetected-second-allele rate in recessive disease; an equity question (are phase-attributable errors higher where LD-based priors were weakest?); generalises to assumption-attributable error rates (penetrance, mosaicism, population rarity), a template the counselling field already runs for de novo mosaicism (PREGCARE, PMC10447403); and an NLP/report-structuring question about eligibility coding at scale.

Significance — anchoring:
PM3's trans requirement and ClinGen phase-unknown handling; the reclassification/reanalysis literature (18% clinically relevant change at five years, PMC10545662) which counts diagnoses gained, never retracted; gene-level complex alleles; AlAbdi's pitfall taxonomy and the ACMG "nine categories of pitfalls" abstract; the missing-second-allele problem.

Reason for silence:
Claimed: (1) new instrument — direct phase at arbitrary separation only became routine with long reads (~500 bp short-read limit; 78.7% of Cao et al.'s pairs beyond it); (2) incentive/accountability gap — only the labs whose reports would be shown wrong hold the archives, DNA and consents, with no regulatory duty to audit and non-zero liability; (3) framing — reanalysis is funded as yield-increasing, so retraction-direction work sits outside the workflow. Gate 4 broke (1) and (3): the question was asked and partly answered by inference in 2023-24, before routine long reads, and Guo's cis cases produced published clinician recontact, i.e. retraction-direction work. Only (2) survives, and it explains silence on the issued-clinical-report framing, not on the substantive question — which the LEDGER's own Gate 4 rule says should send the novelty finding back to Gate 2, exactly where it then failed.

- **Confirmed, and it is the kill.** Among the 293 CMG patients whose presumed-causal pair was in gnomAD, the paper predicts "seven variant pairs (2.4%) to be in *cis*" — six from proband-only sequencing, one from a trio. For the six proband-only cases "the responsible clinician was contacted to ensure phenotype overlap with the disease gene", with parental Sanger or long-read sequencing sought where possible. This is the candidate's quantity, in already-diagnosed patients, published — exactly the kill condition the Gate 2 record had itself pre-stated.
- **Correction to the Gate 2 record.** It differentiated the candidate on the ground that Guo's validation set "is pre-selected for pairs believed to be in trans, the mirror image of the candidate's eligible subset". That is **false**: the authors phased every pair of rare coding or flanking variants within genes observed in the parents of 4,775 trios and compared against transmission-based phasing, with no pre-selection for trans. The record's one stated point of difference does not exist, which makes the Disguise finding stronger than the adversary argued rather than weaker.
- **Residue, stated accurately rather than favourably.** Two things Guo does not deliver: the 2.4% is a *predicted* cis fraction from a population-genetic estimator rather than a long-read measurement on stored DNA — and the paper documents one case where the prediction was wrong, a trio pair predicted cis but confirmed in trans by transmission — and the outcomes of the clinician follow-up on the six proband-only cases are not reported, so no diagnostic error rate is published. That is a better-instrument re-measurement of an answered question plus an unreported follow-up, which under the operating rules is a disguised known ("Rejected even if the exact variant is unmeasured"), not an un-asked question. It is not routed, because the question was answered by another route rather than left open in print.

ID: UQ-20261016-15
Date: 2026-10-16
Status: Rejected — Gate 2 (novelty Low; the gate the candidate failed at, so no adversary was run). Clause (a), that independently published verdicts on the same pair disagree, is already asked and answered in restricted form with a number attached: Neininger 2018 reports 17.1% (6/35) outright contradiction between two databases on shared pairs. Clause (b), the method-sensitivity explanation, is stated in that same paper as the probable cause and left untested, i.e. asked-but-open, not un-asked. What R1 adds over P1 is a unit-of-analysis swap (primary determinations for database entries) plus a matching rule and a chance-corrected statistic on the same corpus — a measurement upgrade on an asked question, which the operating rules treat as a disguised known and reject even though the exact refined variant is unmeasured. The question form is additionally routine one field over (DDI compendium-agreement studies with kappa; USP/PDA/ISPE probability-of-detection and inspector-agreement analysis of visible-particle inspection). Independently of this, well-posedness is 2/3, which also bars Validated; and because no adversary ran, the Disguise attack is unverified — no searches were made in vocabularies Gate 2 did not try — so this entry could not have been Validated in any case.
Domain(s): Medicine — hospital pharmacy, injectable-drug compatibility and drug-information resources; physical chemistry of formulations; measurement-agreement methodology

Question (canonical): Over the published corpus of Y-site physical-compatibility determinations, restricted to drug pairs with >=2 independent primary determinations matched by a pre-specified comparability rule (same drugs and salt forms, concentrations within a factor of two, same diluent class, stated mixing-ratio band, overlapping observation window, same temperature band): (a) what is verdict concordance across matched replicates (percent agreement plus a chance-corrected statistic); (b) does discordance follow a pre-specified detection-sensitivity ordering (visual inspection < pH shift < turbidimetry < sub-visible particle counting; HPLC for the chemical endpoint), i.e. do less sensitive endpoints systematically return "compatible"; (c) how much discordance survives adjustment for concentration ratio, diluent, observation time and proximity to the pair's solubility/pH-precipitation boundary; (d) for discordant pairs, do compendium entries (Trissel's, King Guide, Stabilis, Micromedex IV Compatibility) track the majority verdict or the most sensitive determination?
(Intake V0 asked the same thing without a unit of analysis, a comparability rule or a verdict mapping; R1 above is the single permitted Gate 1 reformulation and is the operative formulation. Full text of both: batches/2026-10-16-0433/UQ-20261016-15-record.md.)

Alternative formulations:
- What is the inter-study reliability of a Y-site compatibility verdict, and what would a compendium entry look like if it carried a confidence rather than a binary call?
- Are "compatible"/"incompatible" labels in injectable-drug compendia properties of the drug pair, or of the sensitivity of the assay used on it?

Motivating gap: Silence mapping. Thousands of pairwise determinations, compendia and ICU co-infusion audits (how-answers) with no question asked about the verdict itself — its reproducibility between independent determinations, and its dependence on detection sensitivity, since visual inspection cannot see sub-visible particulate, so "compatible" may mean "nothing was looked for". Gate 2 partly overturned this gap claim (see below).

Presuppositions:
1. Enough pairs carry >=2 independent primary determinations under matched conditions to estimate concordance — TESTABLE, UNVERIFIED; load-bearing weakness. Gostynska 2024 tables show same-drug C-vs-I conflicts (aminophylline, ampicillin, alprostadil, fosphenytoin, furosemide, ceftazidime), but those conflicts travel with PN formulation, product, concentration and ratio, so strict matching may leave almost no replicates.
2. Reports state method, concentrations, diluent, ratio and window well enough to define "comparable conditions" — CONTESTED (Medicina Intensiva review: pH reported in 44%, HPLC 22%, triplicate 26%; "none of the included studies followed all the methodological requirements").
3. A binary verdict is the field's operative output — ESTABLISHED for compendia, wall charts and alert logic.
4. Sub-visible particulate matters clinically — CONTESTED in magnitude; the candidate needs only that the endpoints are not interchangeable.
5. Discordance is attributable to method/conditions rather than nucleation stochasticity near a metastable boundary — EXPLICITLY NOT ASSUMED; boundary proximity enters limb (c) as a competing explanation.
6. Compendium entries are traceable to primary determinations — CONTESTED; commercial products are not auditable from outside, so limb (d) is feasible mainly for Stabilis and Trissel's reference lists.

What would count as an answer: Extraction of published determinations into a pair x condition x method x verdict table; the matching rule applied to find replicates; percent and chance-corrected agreement on the matched set; regression of discordance on endpoint, concentration ratio, diluent, observation time and boundary proximity; a trace of compendium entries for discordant pairs. Pre-committed readings: "verdicts are assay properties" = substantial, method-ordered discordance; "verdicts are pair properties" = high cross-endpoint concordance, which retires the worry; "not estimable" = too few matched replicates, reported as a coverage result about the literature.

Novelty — queries run (query → one-line result): 11 queries, 5 fetches (one fetch failed); budget cap reached, full list in batches/2026-10-16-0433/UQ-20261016-15-record.md. No adversary ran, so there are no adversary query lists. Most informative:
- Q5 "'compatibility' injectable drugs 'contradictory' OR 'discordant' results between references how often percentage of pairs disagree reproducibility" → DECISIVE: Neininger 2018 (P1), which asks and quantifies the discordance clause.
- Q6 (mandated own-field title form) "reproducibility of Y-site compatibility studies conflicting compatibility reports replicate determination same drug pair hospital pharmacy" → systematic review and single-pair studies only; nothing treating verdict reproducibility as a subject.
- Q7 "comparison of drug compatibility information sources discrepancy rate agreement percentage between references injectable drugs" → returns the DDI-compendium agreement literature instead: the same question form is routine one field over.
- Q9 (pharmaceutical QC vocabulary) "attribute agreement analysis probability of detection visual inspection particulate matter parenteral solutions interlaboratory kappa" → USP/PDA/ISPE probability-of-detection and kappa apparatus fully developed for human visible-particle inspection, never pointed at compatibility verdicts.
- Q10 "Kanji 2010 systematic review physical chemical compatibility ... conflicting results" → did not retrieve; Kanji 2010 remains UNOPENED and is cited only as reported by P1.
Ledger duplicate check: INDEX.md read in full (UQ-20261015-01 … UQ-20261016-10); nearest neighbour UQ-20261016-02 (DDI severity classes audited against measured harm) opened — same genus, different object. No ledger duplicate.

Novelty — nearest prior formulations (3, with sources):
P1. Neininger MP et al., "Incompatibilities in paediatric intensive care — pitfalls in drug information", Die Pharmazie 2018;73:605-608 (opened, full text). 318 PICU pairs; 35 covered by both databases; "in 17.1% (6/35) Database B indicated compatibility whereas Database A indicated incompatibility"; information "incomplete, heterogeneous, and partly contradictory"; contradictions "likely to be caused by the heterogeneity of the methods used to determine incompatibility" (citing Kanji 2010) — asserted, not tested.
P2. "Compatibility of drugs administered as Y-site infusion in intensive care units: A systematic review", Medicina Intensiva, ahead-of-print S2173572719302139 (PMID 30262380; opened at medintensiva.org; authors/volume NOT verified, PubMed returned a captcha, left blank rather than invented). 29 studies, 945 possible pairs, data for 475; endpoints extracted per study; says turbidimetry/microscopy are more accurate than visual observation and underused; reports no study-versus-study disagreement and no agreement statistic.
P3. Gostynska A, Przybylski T, Ogrodowczyk M, Pharmaceutics 2024;16(2):264 (opened). Builds the pair x PN formulation x ratio x verdict table with an A-D evidence grade plus a method table; its tables visibly contain opposite verdicts for the same drug across studies, but it never labels them disagreements, quantifies concordance, or attributes them to endpoint sensitivity.
Lower standing: Linguadoca C et al., EJHP abstract GRP-163 (opened) — 7,488 combinations from six sources, "data collected conflicted in 1.8% of references", no method analysis, no resolution rule. Not opened: PTHP 2017 quality-criteria paper (title/DOAJ only); Kanji et al. 2010 (Crit Care Med), known only via P1.

Novelty — how this differs from each: vs P1 — the candidate swaps the unit of analysis (independent primary determinations instead of two commercial databases' entries), adds a matching rule, a chance-corrected statistic, a boundary-proximity competitor and a compendium-fidelity limb; i.e. it measures what P1 asserts. vs P2 — same corpus and endpoints extracted, but P2 asks a coverage question (how much of the matrix is filled) rather than a reliability one. vs P3 — holds the candidate's own deliverable table and displays the conflicts without computing concordance. vs neighbouring fields — chance-corrected compendium-agreement studies are routine in DDI pharmacology and probability-of-detection/inspector-agreement analysis is standard in pharmaceutical QC, so the question form is an import, not an invention.

Novelty confidence: Low

Significance — consequence: If discordance is substantial and method-ordered, a compendium "compatible" is partly a statement about the assay: entries resting on a single visual-only determination would be labelled untested rather than cleared, the error is directional (false reassurance), and editors would have to choose openly between majority and most-sensitive verdict. If concordance is high, the binary form is vindicated and the insensitivity worry is retired. If too few pairs survive matching, no compendium verdict has ever been independently reproduced under comparable conditions — a stronger statement than either.
Significance — audience: compendium editors and database curators (Trissel's, King Guide, Stabilis/Infostab, Micromedex); P&T committees and pharmacy informatics staff who build co-infusion charts and pump/EHR rules (GRP-163 is a documented instance with its own 1.8% conflict rate resolved by an unstated rule); ICU/neonatal protocol authors; methodologists and reviewers of compatibility studies, who set minimum endpoints; PN guideline groups (ASPEN/ESPEN).
Significance — fecundity: probability-of-detection curves for an incompatibility by endpoint; whether the clinically relevant threshold is visible precipitate or a USP-type sub-visible count; whether source disagreement predicts catheter occlusion or line complications; how much apparent discordance is nucleation stochasticity near a metastable limit; whether single-visual-determination pairs are over-represented among pairs clinicians actually co-infuse.
Significance — anchoring: the "no data available" bucket of ICU co-infusion audits; P1's untested method-heterogeneity conjecture; P2's 26% triplicate rate; USP particulate limits and the visible/sub-visible boundary; the USP/PDA/ISPE inspection-agreement apparatus; alert and chart configuration that consumes a confidence-free binary as if it had one.

Reason for silence: Not "no one thought of it" — P1 thought of it in one sentence and stopped. (1) Incentive and ownership gap: determinations are single-pair service studies consumed through compendia that must emit one binary per pair; the aggregate has no owner, commercial publishers do not expose grading for audit and have no reason to publish a reliability estimate of their own product, and authors are rewarded for adding a pair, not re-measuring one — which is also why replicates are scarce. (2) A practice rule removes the need for the number: "if any source says incompatible, treat as incompatible" turns discordance into an operational nuisance rather than a quantity. (3) Vocabulary boundary: chance-corrected agreement, limit/probability of detection and measurement-system analysis live in lab medicine and pharmaceutical QC, not in the stability-and-compatibility tradition, whose methodology literature is about doing one study well.

Status: Provisional
Domain(s): Medicine — physiology / infectious disease / clinical thermometry. Secondary: measurement metrology; screening epidemiology.
Question (canonical): In a multi-site EHR corpus spanning roughly 1995–2025, restricted to episodes of documented infection (coded syndrome plus culture- or NAAT-confirmed pathogen) and taking as the episode peak the maximum temperature recorded strictly before the first antipyretic administration timestamp, with the contemporaneous reference being the afebrile temperature distribution of non-infected patients in the same health system, device class and time-of-day window: within strata of age band, syndrome, pathogen, severity-at-presentation and device class, is the calendar-year slope of (episode peak − contemporaneous afebrile reference) zero, and how does it compare with the calendar-year slope of the afebrile reference itself? (Additive primary scale, mandatory bounded/multiplicative sensitivity analysis; any pre-1950 archival arm reported only as a bias-bounded estimate.) One Gate 1 reformulation used; intaked version and rationale in the record.
Alternative formulations:
- Is fever amplitude (peak minus that era's own afebrile baseline) in documented infection constant across birth cohorts, or has it declined?
- Of the difference between historical and modern fever observations, how much is a shifted baseline and how much a smaller rise per unit of infectious stimulus?
- Has the acute-phase temperature response per unit of measured stimulus (°C per log CRP, per log pathogen load) changed by calendar year within matched syndrome and device class?
Motivating gap: Anomaly mining. Mean US body temperature has fallen ~0.03 °C per birth decade since the 1890s (Protsiv et al., eLife 2020;9:e49555). The downstream policy limb — should 38.0/38.3 °C be lowered? — is in print as unevidenced conjecture (Wright & Auwaerter, OFID 2020;7(5):ofaa132, Conclusions; quote verified verbatim by both adversaries). The un-asked quantity is the decomposition Δpeak = Δbaseline + Δamplitude, which separates "the ruler moved" (re-referencing restores sensitivity) from "the response weakened" (re-referencing does not). Ledger adjacency: UQ-20261016-13 (in-vitro MIC at site temperature) distinct; UQ-20261016-09 (cross-era biospecimen comparability) same failure mode, Rejected, checked against the archival arm.
Presuppositions: P1 (partly contested) usable historical infection series with stated denominators exist — raw material confirmed digitised, no denominated series found. P2 (CONTESTED) cross-era thermometry comparable after calibration/site/dwell correction; offsets are the same order as the effect — not load-bearing for the modern-era primary arm. P3 (CONTESTED) cohorts matchable across eras on syndrome/severity/age. P4 (contested) pre-antipyretic peak identifiable from EHR administration timestamps. P5 (CONTESTED, physiological) "amplitude" defined independently of baseline — assumes additive set-point displacement; set-point-vs-gain is live and actively revised (Romanovsky, PMID 15970487), so the Gate 1 scale pre-specification is a repair of statement, not of physiology. P6 (CONTESTED) the secular baseline fall is real, not instrument artefact (disputed by Jones, SBM 2020) — the reformulated question does not inherit it. P7 (deduction against well-posedness) peak attained is a function of amplitude, stimulus magnitude AND time allowed before truncation; earlier presentation and earlier antimicrobials lower observed peak with no physiological change, so a negative Δamplitude is unidentified unless time-from-onset and a stimulus measure are conditioned on. P8 (added by adversary #1) both slopes are estimable at useful precision inside one instrument era.
What would count as an answer: A calendar-year-stratified distribution of pre-antipyretic peak in matched documented infection with thermometric bias carried as a term with uncertainty, yielding Δpeak decomposed into Δbaseline and Δamplitude with intervals on the pre-specified scale plus bounded-scale sensitivity analysis, conditioned on time-from-onset and a stimulus measure (P7). "Baseline only" if the Δamplitude interval contains zero while Δbaseline is clearly negative; "response attenuation" if Δamplitude is clearly negative and survives that conditioning; a null bounded away from |Δamplitude| < 0.2 °C also answers it. Feasible without any archival arm.
Novelty — queries run (query → one-line result): Gate 2: ledger duplicate check (INDEX.md, 49 entries — no duplicate or near-duplicate) plus 11 distinct web searches at the session cap, across lay, technical, historical, veterinary, metrological and screening-epidemiology vocabularies and the answer side; none returned an on-point paper. Most informative: "secular trend in peak temperature during documented infection historical versus modern cohorts" → anchors only; "has the febrile response attenuated over time … birth cohort" → age-blunting review (PMC7740114) and pregnancy/endotoxin blunting, nothing era-stratified; "temporal trend maximum body temperature sepsis pneumonia EHR decline over decade" → within-episode trajectory phenotyping only; "cross-era thermometry comparability mercury versus electronic offset bias" → supplies P2's offset magnitudes, never applied across eras; "height of fever in lobar pneumonia historical case series compared with contemporary patients" → digitised 19th-c. lectures, no cross-era comparison. CAVEAT: the bibliographic arm did not execute — Europe PMC proxy-blocked, 2 of 3 PubMed fetches failed, Protsiv unopenable at Gate 2. Gate 4 added 18 further queries (9 per adversary) in German, Spanish, French, controlled-human-infection, vaccine-reactogenicity, pyrogen-physiology, history-of-medicine, wearable-thermometry, acute-phase and own-field EHR-title vocabularies; the only on-point neighbour surfaced was Niven CCM 2013 (adversary #1, query 7). Database access failed again for both adversaries (PubMed reCAPTCHA; eutils CONNECT 403), so no bibliographic database has ever been queried for this candidate. Full lists: batches/2026-10-16-0633/UQ-20261016-16-record.md, UQ-20261016-16-adversary-1.md, UQ-20261016-16-adversary-2.md.
Novelty — nearest prior formulations (3, with sources):
1. Protsiv M, Ley C, Lankester J, Hastie T, Parsonnet J. "Decreasing human body temperature in the United States since the Industrial Revolution." eLife 2020;9:e49555 (PMC6946399) — READ IN FULL by adversary #2.
2. Niven DJ et al. "Fever in Adult ICUs: An Interrupted Time Series Analysis." Crit Care Med 2013 (3 Calgary ICUs, 2004–2009; proportion of admissions with fever >38.3 °C fell from ~1/2 to ~1/4) — identified by adversary #1 via the Alberta Health Services release; full text NOT read (PubMed reCAPTCHA). Unlogged by Gate 2.
3. Wright WF, Auwaerter PG. "Fever and Fever of Unknown Origin." Open Forum Infect Dis 2020;7(5):ofaa132 (PMC7237822) — READ IN FULL by both adversaries; quoted Conclusions sentence verified verbatim.
Further neighbours (not priors): Jones C, "Are humans cooling? Probably not," Science-Based Medicine 2020 (read at Gate 2); "Altered Febrile Responses in Older Adults," PMC7740114 (titles only); Gurven et al., Sci Adv 2020 (press only); clinicalcorrelations.org, "The Myth of 98.6 Fahrenheit," Mar 2026 (read by adversary #2).
Novelty — how this differs from each:
1. vs Protsiv — CORRECTION to the Gate 2 record, which claimed Protsiv "reports no temperatures from documented infection episodes": false. It reports UAVCW means for malaria, syphilis, hepatitis, tuberculosis, pneumonia and cystitis (TB 37.22 °C, pneumonia 37.06 °C vs 37.02 °C comparison). The true difference is that these are fever-screened ("any observations having a diagnosis of fever at the time of the medical examination were excluded … irrespective of the temperature measurement at the visit"), censored at >39 °C, non-peak means with no same-site/same-device modern comparator — i.e. Δbaseline only, with the febrile tail deliberately removed.
2. vs Niven — dichotomised fever incidence >38.3 °C across all ICU admissions over 6 years: no documented-infection matching, no pathogen/syndrome strata, no contemporaneous afebrile reference, no pre-antipyretic peak, no baseline/amplitude decomposition. A close neighbour on calendar-time fever decline in a clinical population, at far coarser resolution, and the strongest evidence that the confounders in P7 are large.
3. vs Wright & Auwaerter — asks the downstream policy question and answers it by conjecture; verified to contain no era-stratified peak data, no fever-magnitude analysis, and to propose a revised population normal value rather than contemporaneous or per-person referencing (adding that this "will likely require a high-profile effort such as a National Academy of Science–sponsored study").
Novelty confidence: Medium. **Judge's post-Gate-5 verification (2026-10-16, independent fresh-context sweep, 21 deliberately varied queries plus the mandatory own-field-title queries, 1 safety refusal):** no study stratifying fever peak by era within a matched infection was found in any vocabulary. Protsiv et al. (eLife 2020;9:e49555) was read in full via PMC6946399 and is afebrile-baseline-only *by explicit construction* — "any observations having a diagnosis of fever at the time of the medical examination were excluded", and ">39C" excluded as "implausible or ... indicated a diagnosis of fever" — i.e. it discards precisely the observations this candidate is about. Wright & Auwaerter (OFID 2020;7(5):ofaa132) was read and is conjecture only, with no era data on fever height; its historical material concerns the *definition* of fever (Wunderlich 38.0C, Petersdorf-Beeson 38.3C, Mackowiak 36.8C mean), not how high fevers peaked. The closest thing located is Gurven et al., Sci Adv 2020;6(44):eabc6599 (Tsimane): infection "explain[s] variation in BT" but "these factors do not account for the temporal declines" — it tests whether infection explains the *baseline* decline, over 16 years of one cohort, and never compares antipyretic-naive peaks across eras. Also opened and ruled out: medRxiv 2021.06.13.21258846 (fever cut-off recalibration on subjective febrile sensation, no documented infection, no era arm); "Altered Febrile Responses in Older Adults" (PMC7740114) and PMID 11523629, the nearest febrile-attenuation work, both on the AGE axis with no era comparison and no temperatures quantified; Markota et al., Front Physiol 2023;14:1215686 (therapeutic hyperthermia, no secular claim). Held at Medium rather than raised to High for two reasons: coverage is web-search-grade, not database-grade (the egress proxy refused CONNECT to Europe PMC REST and NCBI eutils, a PubMed query returned HTTP 429 with an instruction not to retry, PMC served a reCAPTCHA on one fetch and a safety filter refused another, and elifesciences.org and science.org are JavaScript-walled), so Gate 2 is **partially satisfied, not satisfied**; and the threshold neighbour sits close. The novelty claim is narrowed accordingly: it is NOT unasked whether the temperature decline survives adjustment for infection — Gurven et al. ask exactly that and answer that it does. What is unasked is this decomposition: peak attained during matched documented infection, antipyretic-naive, minus the contemporaneous afebrile baseline, compared across eras.
Grading: 11 + 18 = 29 documented queries, no on-point decomposition, and the two nearest full texts plus the field's newest review read and confirmed not to pose it. Held at Medium, not raised: a previously unlogged close neighbour (Niven 2013) fell out of adversary #1's first well-aimed query, and no bibliographic database has been reachable in three sessions, so the instrument that would settle novelty has never been run. Not Low: no near-duplicate; the decomposition against a contemporaneous afebrile reference was found nowhere.
Significance — consequence: If Δamplitude ≈ 0 while Δbaseline < 0 ("ruler moved"), the deficit is metrological and fever criteria should be re-referenced to a contemporaneous or per-person baseline in SD units. If Δamplitude is clearly negative ("response weakened"), re-referencing does not restore sensitivity and the implication is secular change in innate immune activation or set-point regulation. A bounded null (|Δamplitude| < 0.2 °C) closes the ambiguity cheaply.
Significance — audience: Bodies setting fever criteria (AAP febrile-infant 38.0 °C, Sepsis-3/SIRS, IDSA/NCCN neutropenic-fever 38.3/38.0 °C, FUO definitions, CDC/WHO entry screening); the clinical-thermometry standards community (ISO 80601-2-56, tympanic and temporal-artery vendors) for bias budgets against a drifting population mean; EHR CDS builders firing sepsis alerts on temperature thresholds (adjacent to UQ-20261015-21); thermoregulation physiologists and inflammaging immunologists. Contested at Gate 4: see Strongest remaining objection.
Significance — fecundity: (a) °C of rise per unit measured stimulus by calendar year — the cleaner estimand and natural follow-on; (b) has the whole acute-phase response (HR, WBC, ESR, CRP) attenuated, decomposed the same way; (c) does antipyretic availability change first the measured and then the actual fever curve; (d) within-person fever delta by birth cohort from continuous wearable thermometry; (e) veterinary replication where records are long and instrument-stable; (f) adversary #2's unexploited source — febrile response magnitude in controlled human infection models from the 1960s to now, where stimulus is fixed by design and P7 does not bite.
Significance — anchoring: The Protsiv/Gurven secular-decline anomaly and its unresolved instrument-artefact dispute; the blunted-fever-in-the-elderly literature as a confounder whose era analogue is unexamined; Wright & Auwaerter's open threshold conjecture; the long-standing complaint that SIRS/Sepsis-3 temperature criteria are miscalibrated; the higher mortality of afebrile sepsis presentation, whose reading depends on whether afebrility is spreading for mechanical or physiological reasons; the set-point-vs-gain dispute in thermal physiology.
Reason for silence: Primary mechanism (WITHDRAWN at Gate 4): the record's claim that the quantity became computable only with mature EHR corpora is falsified by Niven doing a calendar-time clinical fever analysis on 2004–2009 data. Surviving and now concretely evidenced — disciplinary/design boundary: the team best placed to ask held both terms and discarded the febrile observations by design, excluding any visit with a fever diagnosis irrespective of the measured temperature and censoring above 39 °C (Protsiv, read by adversary #2); a design whose validity depends on excluding fever cannot pose a question about fever magnitude, and the papers inheriting it (Wright & Auwaerter 2020; the Mar-2026 review) inherit the exclusion. Also surviving: a ready local explanation (age, immunosuppression) absorbs each weak-fever observation before the era form of the question can be posed; and no sponsor — a secular trend in peak fever sponsors no trial, drug or product. Not claimed: "no one thought of it".
Adversarial log (8 rows: attack | objection | response | status): Two independent fresh-context adversaries (A1, A2), 9 new queries and 4 fetches each; worse status governs. **Judge's post-Gate-5 note:** A1's Partial on attack 2 (Disguise) rested on its bibliographic arm never having executed in three sessions. That arm has now been executed independently (see Novelty confidence above) and returned no duplicate, so Disguise is no longer the reason Validated is unavailable. What keeps this entry Provisional is Gate 1 well-posedness 2/3 (below the 3/3 Validated requires) and the Unresolved status on attack 6, significance inflation. A confound no located prior has handled, logged here because the question must handle it: era-stratified peak comparison is confounded by thermometry site and instrument (mercury oral/axillary versus tympanic/temporal-artery), and Protsiv's own >39C exclusion means the most-cited secular dataset cannot be reused for the febrile tail. Verbatim logs: UQ-20261016-16-adversary-1.md, UQ-20261016-16-adversary-2.md.

Two full texts read; neither contains the calendar-year slope of (peak − contemporaneous reference), and the limbs have opposite policy consequences. | Resolved (A1 Resolved, A2 Resolved) |
| 2 Disguise | It is the known critical-care question "why is observed fever disappearing?" renamed — Niven CCM 2013 asked a calendar-time clinical fever-decline question in 2013 and Gate 2's 11 queries missed it (A1); or "has temperature at presentation fallen / has the acute-phase response attenuated?" renamed (A2). | Niven's estimand is dichotomised incidence over all ICU admissions with no infection matching, no contemporaneous reference and no decomposition; 18 fresh queries in nine vocabularies, including the obvious own-field EHR title form, returned no on-point decomposition, and Protsiv, Wright & Auwaerter and the Mar-2026 review were read and demonstrably do not pose it. | PARTIAL (A1 Partial — "do not read this as passed"; A2 Resolved with caveat). | 3 Combinatorial novelty | Secular-trend epidemiology × clinical thermometry, the only new object being an arithmetic subtraction of two published slopes. | Real interface problem: the two terms sit in different populations with different device mixes and different truncation processes, so constructing a contemporaneous afebrile reference within device class and hour, and identifying a pre-antipyretic peak, are the substance of the design. P7 is an obstruction, not boilerplate. | Resolved (both) |
| 4 Presupposition failure | An unlisted P8: that both slopes are estimable at useful precision within one instrument era — Protsiv's rate implies Δbaseline of only 0.05–0.1 °C across 1995–2025, while Niven shows care-process change moved recorded clinical fever by an order of magnitude more in six years; the birth-cohort escape re-imports age–period–cohort non-identifiability (A1). P5 is worse than flagged: set-point-vs-gain is contested (Romanovsky, PMID 15970487), so Δpeak = Δbaseline + Δamplitude may decompose nothing physiological, and Protsiv's 39 °C ceiling shows the febrile tail is routinely censored even in baseline work (A2). | Large n with strata on device class, site and hour; bias terms pre-specified; a reported bound rather than a point estimate is permitted; the estimand is defined whatever physiology turns out to be, and P5 is flagged contested as Gate 1 requires. | Partial (both). Scores: Well-posedness 2/3 · Significance 2/3
Well-posedness 2/3 (carried from Gate 1, unchanged at Gate 5): the quantity is measurable, the estimand's scale is pre-specified, the answer criteria include a reportable bound, and every presupposition is explicit; one point withheld for P7 — the measurement is well-posed, its physiological reading is not, and P5 is repaired by statement rather than resolved. Gate 4 adds no reason to raise it and supplies P8 against it. Significance 2/3 as recorded, now carrying an Unresolved objection that the branches do not fork any named decision.
Strongest remaining objection: The effect sought is smaller than the noise and smaller than the decision grain — Protsiv's rate implies ~0.05–0.1 °C of Δbaseline across the whole feasible 1995–2025 window, which is below the pre-specified "clinically meaningful" null band of 0.2 °C, an order of magnitude below the care-process movement Niven documents in six years in one health system (ICU fever >38.3 °C, ~50% to ~25% of admissions), and below the 0.3 °C grain at which guideline thresholds step; so the P7 confounders dominate the only feasible arm, the bounded null is near-guaranteed and uninformative, and both branches leave every named audience doing the same thing (lower or individualise the cut-off). This is the Unresolved significance-inflation attack and adversary #1's magnitude objection stated as one objection.
Promotion requires: (i) naming at least one identified decision-maker whose action differs between the two branches — not two branches — e.g. a CDS or ISO bias-budget calibration whose numeric output changes; (ii) an executed bibliographic pass on a real database (PubMed/Embase/Scopus, not generic web search) covering "proportion afebrile at presentation" period trends in febrile neutropenia, febrile infants and bacteraemia, with Niven CCM 2013 read in full and treated as a prior; and (iii) a power and device-drift budget showing the reference slope is estimable within one instrument era at precision finer than the effect sought, with a null band narrower than the ~0.1 °C the baseline literature predicts; (iv) for 3/3 well-posedness, a design that conditions on time-from-symptom-onset and a stimulus measure so the immunological limb is identified. Validated also requires the bibliographic arm in (ii) to have run at all, which it has not in three sessions.
Suggested first step toward an answer (pointer only — do not take it): Not taken. The pointer is a feasibility scoping pass, not the analysis: in one multi-site EHR, quantify the device-class mix and antipyretic-timestamp completeness by calendar year, then estimate the attainable precision on the afebrile reference slope before any peak is extracted — if that slope is not estimable below ~0.05 °C, the contrast cannot be formed and the question should be re-posed as the per-unit-stimulus version or moved to controlled human infection models, where stimulus is fixed by design.
Routing (if rejected as already-asked): Not rejected, so not routed. Noted for the record: the downstream threshold limb — "should 38.0/38.3 °C be lowered given the secular fall in baseline?" — is asked-but-open in print (Wright & Auwaerter, OFID 2020;7(5):ofaa132, Conclusions, verified verbatim by both adversaries) and belongs in ledger/routed-open-problems.md on its own account; it is a different question from this candidate's decomposition and is not this entry's routing.

ID: UQ-20261016-17
Date: 2026-10-16
Status: Rejected
Domain(s): Medicine / STEM — biological standardisation and metrology in laboratory medicine; pharmacopoeial science. Neighbours engaged: physical metrology (BIPM/JCTLM), index-number economics (chain drift), haemostasis standardisation.
Question (canonical): For WHO International Standards now on their third or later generation with publicly retrievable collaborative-study reports, (a) what is the product across replacements of the discrepancy between each study's estimated potency ratio to the outgoing standard and the unitage actually assigned to the incoming one, (b) what is the convolution across replacements of the published per-study dispersions that the continuity convention sets to zero, and (c) do (a)+(b) exceed the tolerance of the named IU-denominated clinical cut-offs and pharmacopoeial potency limits for those analytes, and the routine reproducibility of the assays applying them? (Gate 1 reformulation; the Gate 0 wording — "how far has the realised IU drifted from its original definition" — was superseded because the continuity convention makes that point estimate identically zero by construction.)
Alternative formulations: (1) Is the IU of a biological metrologically continuous across standard generations, or is today's IU an undocumented random walk from the first standard? (2) What is the total uncertainty of "1 IU" today if every replacement's calibration uncertainty is carried forward instead of zeroed? (3) Is WHO's mandated per-replacement continuity evaluation sufficient to bound the cumulative deviation of the realised IU, or does its per-standard scope make portfolio-level deviation unobservable in principle?
Motivating gap: Presupposition inversion. Replacements are value-assigned against the predecessor in a collaborative study; the assigned unitage is then treated as exact to keep the unit "continuous" and the study's dispersion is not propagated. Standards for hormones, coagulation factors and heparin are on their 2nd–6th generation while every IU-denominated threshold (anti-HBs 10 IU/L, FVIII potency labelling, hCG, anti-D) behaves as if the unit were fixed. The field has a per-replacement check and no cumulative account — so the claim is "never aggregated", not "never noticed". Gate 4 found the motivating anomaly to be misread (see below).
Presuppositions: P1 replacement calibrated against predecessor with a published ratio + dispersion — partly confirmed (Gray 2017), contested for oldest generations. P2 assigned unitage stated without uncertainty — historically true, now policy-false (Bristow ID-909: WHO recommendations revised 2004 require an uncertainty statement and a continuity evaluation, per replacement). P3 chain is linear and documented — partly falsified: multi-parent bridging (Poller 2005), re-anchoring (HPLC-assigned GH) and chain splitting (1988 FSH) are documented. P4 IU-denominated thresholds would move with the unit — supported for named cases, but adversary 1 showed reagent/platform calibration and commutability dominate for anti-HBs. P5 drift is confounded with artefact degradation — confirmed live and acknowledged in-field. P6 published dispersion estimates bridging error — contested and unresolved: NIBSC's own account makes GCV a mixture of assay imprecision and method bias. **New at Gate 4 (fatal):** the rounding premise behind estimand (a) ("500 IU/ampoule, 10 IU/ampoule") is uncited and is contradicted by the record's own assignments (0.86 U/ampoule; 130 and 173 IU/mg, i.e. 2–3 significant figures); and across the candidate's flagship chain the source material changes (bovine lung → porcine mucosa), so the ratio across that step has no common referent.
What would count as an answer: Per-analyte chain reconstruction from the public collaborative-study record — product of assigned-versus-estimated residuals as cumulative systematic deviation, convolution of consensus-potency standard errors as cumulative uncertainty, both compared to each IU-denominated decision threshold's tolerance and to routine assay CV. Three outcomes: small relative to assay CV (convention vindicated with numbers); large for named standards (generation-tag or re-anchor them); record too incomplete for the oldest chains (documented coverage gap addressed to WHO ECBS and custodian laboratories).
Novelty — queries run (query → one-line result): 11 at Gate 2 (cap 11) + 9 by adversary 1 + 9 by adversary 2 = 29 distinct, across lay, pharmacopoeial, historical, German, French, NAT-unitage, CRM-recertification, EQA, IVD-metrology and index-number vocabularies. Full lists: batches/2026-10-16-0633/UQ-20261016-17-record.md and the two adversary files. Most informative: own-field title query (`comparison of successive WHO international standards potency has the International Unit drifted heparin 1941 Barrowcliffe`) → heparin standard-series reviews plus the USP heparin unit-harmonisation statement (fetch failed at Gate 2 and never opened by either adversary); `"chain drift" chained index number theory accumulated error` → chain drift is a named, remedied problem in index-number economics with no contact with calibration chains; `retrospective comparison all previous generations of a WHO International Standard assayed against the current standard` (adversary 2, answer-side) → the Gray deck, i.e. the all-generations re-assay already executed; `heparin International Standard 1941 to 2008 ... USP unit 2009 change clinical dosing consequence` (adversary 1) → FDA Q&A quantifying the USP→IU harmonisation at ~10% with an explicit clinical-tolerance judgement; `certified reference material recertification successive batches ... cumulative uncertainty` (adversary 2) → value-transfer uncertainty propagation across renewal lots is routine, owned practice in chemical metrology. No portfolio-level audit of WHO standards found in any vocabulary.
Novelty — nearest prior formulations (3, with sources): 1. Poller L et al., "A multicentre calibration study of WHO international reference preparations for thromboplastin, rabbit (RBT/90) and human (rTF/95)", J Clin Pathol 2005;58(6):667–669 (PMID 15917425; PMC1770687 — citation metadata verified by both adversaries, contents captcha-gated for all three passes, so its ISI/INR-bias figures are unverified). 2. van den Besselaar AMHP & Bertina RM, Thromb Haemost 1993;69(1):35–40, DOI 10.1055/s-0038-1651544 (opened and verified by adversary 2; supplies per-step calibration CVs 1.6–5.1%). 3. Gray E., "Value assignment of International Standards: challenges for potency labelling of biotechnology/biosimilar products", GaBI Scientific Meetings 2017 (gabi-journal.net/wp-content/uploads/Gray-V17I08.pdf; opened and verified by adversary 2). Fourth, decisive on the convention: Bristow A. (NIBSC), "Establishing International Units (IU) and the challenges of moving to the SI", BIPM/JCTLM working document ID-909.

ID: UQ-20261016-18
Date: 2026-10-16
Status: Provisional
Domain(s): Medicine — critical care, patient safety, clinical informatics. Transplanted from human-operator control theory / aerospace human factors (describing-function analysis, pilot-induced oscillation); neighbours: process control, human intermittent-control motor neuroscience.

Question (canonical): In adult ICU patients on continuous norepinephrine, with device-integrated pump-rate logs and timestamped pressure at >=4x the hypothesised cadence frequency: (a) does the pump-rate series carry excess band-limited power, and the dose-to-MAP cross-spectrum coherence with loop-consistent phase, in a narrow band centred on the unit's documented assessment/charting cadence (1 h => 2.8e-4 Hz; 2 h => 1.4e-4 Hz), against a pre-specified surrogate noise floor (phase-randomised, block-shuffled) and control band; (b) does that centre frequency move with cadence across units or exogenous protocol/staffing changes; (c) does cadence-band dose-oscillation amplitude predict organ dysfunction (delta SOFA components, new RRT) net of time-weighted mean dose, severity, phenotype and procedure-driven periodicity? [V2, the single permitted Gate 1 reformulation; V1 said "limit-cycle oscillation tracking charting cadence" — see record.]

Alternative formulations: (1) Is bedside vasopressor titration a stable controller, or is there a clinician-induced oscillation — the ICU analogue of pilot-induced oscillation — whose frequency is set by how often the nurse looks? (2) Does the dose-pressure loop show a spectral peak at the charting interval rather than a physiological frequency, and does that peak carry prognostic information? (3) Identify the describing function of the human titrator from clinical logs: gain, effective lag, remnant, phase margin at the sampling frequency.

Motivating gap: Cross-field transplant. Aerospace and process control routinely identify the human operator as a controller and name its failure modes (PIO, hunting, deadband cycling). Critical care is building closed-loop MAP/norepinephrine control (NCT03515161, NCT04106791, NCT04586218, COMAT) on the premise that manual titration performs worse, while comparing devices to manual care only on outcome summaries (time in target, hypotension burden, dose totals) and never identifying the incumbent manual loop's dynamics.

Presuppositions: P1 log resolution finer than the hypothesised period (established with device-integrated pumps + arterial line; made an inclusion criterion in V2). P2 CONTESTED and load-bearing: cadence is exogenous to patient state, so controller and plant are partially separable. P3 CONTESTED: oscillation, if present, is harmful (could be benign or adaptive probing for the weaning point). P4 largely established: physiological rhythms separate in frequency — true for Mayer waves, not for slow drift or sedation/turning/suctioning periodicity. P5 CONTESTED: charted pressure reflects what the clinician saw (charting-time bias corrupts phase). P6 CONTESTED: a prognostic association is not reverse causation from instability. P7 (Gate 1): pump logs record commanded, not delivered, dose; line dead-volume and carrier flow can generate cycling independently. P8 (surfaced by the adversary, never listed, FALSE as used): that a loop sampled every T can express an oscillation of period T.

What would count as an answer: Spectral and describing-function analysis of paired dose and pressure series from >=2 institutions with different documented cadences; pre-registered band, surrogate floor, control band, covariates and endpoint. Positive = cadence-band excess power above floor and control band, coherence with loop-consistent phase, centre frequency that moves when cadence moves exogenously, share of patient-hours in the oscillatory regime, estimated gain and lag, plus an outcome model identified off the cadence contrast. A clean negative settles it equally and retires one implicit justification for closed-loop devices.

Novelty — queries run (query -> one-line result): 12 at Gate 2 (cap was 11; the overshoot is self-reported in the record), 9 new-vocabulary queries by adversary 1 — full lists in batches/2026-10-16-0633/UQ-20261016-18-record.md and batches/2026-10-16-0633/UQ-20261016-18-adversary-1.md. Most informative: "closed-loop vasopressor control versus manual nurse titration performance oscillation hypotension time in target range" -> device-vs-manual trials compare time-in-target only, manual arm never characterised as a controller (confirms the gap). "norepinephrine dose variability predicts mortality septic shock" and "frequency of vasopressor dose changes per hour ICU retrospective MIMIC" (own-field title-form) -> variability means between-patient dose level; titration characterised by targets and protocol, never by timing or spectrum. "\"deadband\" OR \"hunting\" manual control intermittent sampling operator feedback loop cycling" -> mature human intermittent-control theory, applied to posture and tracking, never to titration. "vasopressor dose fluctuation index ... independent of mean dose" (answer-side) -> dose-trajectory-vs-AKI (PMC12074548), not oscillation amplitude. "\"describing function\" OR \"crossover model\" human operator ... drug titration loop identification EHR" -> method exists, no clinical application. Adversary, new vocabularies: German "Regelkreis Pflegekraft Katecholamin ... Messintervall" -> catecholamine syringe/pump changeover perturbs BP (PMC12567164, PMC4840124, NCT01127152), an institution-set nursing cadence already documented to move pressure (titles only; reCAPTCHA). Neonatal "manual FiO2 adjustment frequency SpO2 oscillation ... nurse adjustment interval" -> "Quicker response results in better SpO2 control: a comparison of 3 FiO2 titration strategies" (PMID 26706983), the operator-interval question asked and answered experimentally one organ system away (not opened). "sampled-data human controller limit cycle period equal to sampling interval" -> intermittent-control corpus (arXiv 1705.08228; ar5iv 1407.3543; Gawthrop frequency-domain analysis) giving minimum limit-cycle period 2T. "timing distribution of nurse-initiated norepinephrine dose adjustments" -> reached the record's unopened prior via ivteam.com/?p=253609. Also searched and empty: bullwhip/periodic-review ordering, warfarin INR control, Lomb-Scargle cadence artefact, MIMIC-IV infusion-rate periodogram, French.

Novelty — nearest prior formulations (3, with sources): (1) Sarraf E, "The drug titration paradox: a control engineering perspective", Curr Opin Anaesthesiol 2024;37(4):362-370 — abstract read; titration framed as control, "understanding in its infancy", no oscillation, sampling interval or loop identification. (2) St-Arnaud C et al., "Prescribed targets for titration of vasopressors in septic shock", CMAJ Open 2013;1(4):E127-E133 — full text read; measures whether a target was prescribed and whether it changed, explicitly not whether achieved pressure matched it; no doses, no dose changes, no reassessment timing, no outcomes. (3) Hunter, Manias & Considine (attributed), "Nurse management of noradrenaline infusions in intensive care units: an observational study", PMID 30513357 — abstract obtained by the adversary at ivteam.com/?p=253609 (date discrepancy 2018-19 vs 2023 unresolved; Unimelb record and PMC blocked by bot walls). Two Melbourne ICUs, 14 nurse-patient dyads, ~25 h of paired BP and noradrenaline dose; reports BP "fluctuated constantly" while nurses documented hourly, and names that mismatch as a problem for titration. No dose-change frequency, period, spectrum or outcomes. Fourth (mechanism source, not opened): the Gawthrop/Loram/Lakie intermittent-control line.

Novelty — how this differs from each: vs (1) population-level cross-sectional dose-effect artefact vs a within-patient, frequency-resolved property of the operator loop with a named predicted frequency and a phase requirement; different domain and method. vs (2) that study measures the setpoint half of the loop and leaves actuation and dynamics unmeasured — the candidate is its complement, using cadence rather than target as the exogenous variation. vs (3) closer than the record assumed: it observes the candidate's premise (continuous fluctuation vs hourly documentation driving titration) and flags it, but answers none of the three limbs. vs (4) the mechanism is established in 1-10 Hz psychomotor tasks; the candidate moves it 3-4 orders of magnitude slower, where the sampling interval is written-down institutional policy rather than a neural property — and that same literature is what defeats V2's band (see Attack 4).

Novelty confidence: Medium (minus). Twelve own-field and neighbour-field queries plus nine fresh-vocabulary adversary queries found no formulation of the three-limb question and no answer to it; the closed-loop literature confirms the gap by never characterising the manual arm. Held below High and discounted within Medium by: an unread experimental analogue in a sibling manual loop (neonatal FiO2 response interval), an unread literature in which an institution-set nursing cadence already moves BP (syringe changeover), and prior (3) sitting on the candidate's premise. Novelty is not what rejects this entry.

Significance — consequence: If yes, assessment cadence becomes a modifiable determinant of haemodynamic stability — an intervention needing no device, no capital, no regulatory pathway — and a class of observed dose variability is reattributed from patient to controller. If no (clean negative at both institutions), one implicit justification for closed-loop devices is retired and the device case must rest on workload, adherence and night-shift reliability. If a peak is present but benign (P3 fails), dose probing is shown to be a feature of competent manual control, a direct warning to designers whose cost functions penalise it.

Significance — audience: (i) closed-loop haemodynamic-management developers and trialists (live NCTs named), who would gain a mechanistic comparator and a defensible cost function; (ii) ICU nursing leadership and quality committees, who set cadence and ratios on workload and documentation grounds with no haemodynamic evidence; (iii) critical-care human-factors researchers, who imported aviation's checklists and CRM but not the operator-as-controller method; (iv) ICU data-quality groups, for whom cadence periodicity is currently a nuisance filter; (v) regulators and payers assessing automated titration claims. Discount, conceded in the record and upheld by the adversary: (i) is small and would proceed regardless, (ii) acts on staffing economics, so the effect would have to be large.

Significance — fecundity: The same identification across the other manual ICU loops (insulin/glucose, sedation, FiO2/PEEP, CRRT, inotropes); whether identified gain varies with nurse-patient ratio, shift, seniority or titration authority; a per-unit "loop quality" indicator from archived logs; whether controller-generated oscillation mediates part of the mechanism-free nurse-staffing-to-outcomes association; admissibility of a stepped-wedge randomisation of cadence; what a closed-loop device should imitate versus avoid; ward-level loops with coarser cadence.

Significance — anchoring: The drug titration paradox; MAP-target trials (SEPSISPAM, the 65 trial) whose estimands are means while the dynamics around the target go unmeasured; the closed-loop justification gap; the missing mechanism in nurse-staffing-to-outcomes work; ICU vital-sign data-quality work (hourly-vitals errors, charting-time bias) converted from limitation to measurement target; the dose-variability prognostic literature.

Reason for silence: Partly holds, partly refuted. Holding: (i) asymmetric disciplinary import — critical care took aviation's social and procedural technologies, not the operator-as-transfer-function method, which lives in control journals that reward controller design over measuring incumbent human performance (no clinical describing-function or loop-identification study found in 21 queries); (ii) instrument timing — minute-resolution commanded-dose logs linked to continuous pressure became retrievable only recently, and the common hourly-charted substrate aliases the signal. Refuted or weakened: (iii) the "analysts detrend the band away" mechanism is speculative, and the premise was in fact raised in qualitative nursing vocabulary (prior 3) and the operator-interval question asked and answered experimentally in neonatal oxygen control. The pattern is non-translation of a quantitative method, not silence about the phenomenon — and the more parsimonious reason is that "you act when you look" is regarded as obvious, which is Attack 1 as a sociological fact.
