ID: UQ-20261017-16
Date: 2026-10-17
Status: Rejected
Domain(s): Medicine — prehospital/resuscitation care and systems-of-care quality measurement (target field). Adjacent: clinical informatics / healthcare technology management; measurement-error statistics and time metrology.
Question (canonical): In registries and quality programmes that assemble each case's timeline from timestamps generated by independent clocks (CAD dispatch, monitor/defibrillator, EMS ePCR, ED triage, inpatient EHR, lab analyser), what is the distribution of inter-source clock offsets, and how much does that offset distribution attenuate or distort the estimated per-minute dependence of outcome on elapsed time from which time-critical-care targets are set?
Alternative formulations: (1) How wrong are the clocks that make up a cardiac-arrest or stroke timeline, and what does that error do to the per-minute survival decrement used to justify response-time targets? (2) Treating a time-critical-care timeline as a composite measurement by several uncalibrated instruments, what is the measurement-error model for its timestamps and what bias does it impose on estimated time-dependence? (Gate 1 reformulation, retained in full in the record, names the source pairs, the traceable-UTC reference and the three estimands (a) per-pair signed offset, (b) share traceably synchronised, (c) slope/CI change under regression calibration or SIMEX.)
Motivating gap: As submitted — "synchronisation is assumed as a precondition and the offset itself is never measured" (Campbell, Ann Emerg Med 1995;26:697-701, links CAD and defibrillator stamps and claims only that synchronised clocks "may provide a method of accurately measuring the time elapsed"). FALSIFIED AT GATE 2: the offset has been measured against a traceable reference in this setting (Brabrand 2012), quantified inside one CAD (Srour & Badr 2017), reviewed as an error class (Goodwin 2022), and engineered around in industry since 1996 (US5749902).
Presuppositions: (1) one physical timeline per case, so per-source offset is well defined — ESTABLISHED. (2) Contributing clocks not already traceably synchronised — PARTLY TRUE for human-read and defibrillator clocks (Brabrand: 2/11 ED, 4/11 ambulance within 1 min; max spread 19:05), FALSE for at least some CAD (Srour & Badr: NTP from GPS), and further weakened by sync-at-download in defibrillator data workflows (US5749902, 1996). (3) Offsets recoverable retrospectively — CONTESTED; only the prospective route is shown feasible. (4) Published per-minute estimates are fitted on multi-clock timestamps — FAILS for the headline slope (Utstein 2024 core "Response time" runs PSAP call-connect → arrival at scene, both dispatch-domain); holds only for supplemental multi-clock intervals (call-to-first-shock, EMS-to-ED hand-off). (5) Offsets non-negligible at minutes scale — CONTESTED; doubtful for server-written stamps. (6) Offset not caused by outcome — CONTESTED; correctly separated from charting latency.
What would count as an answer: An empirically estimated per-source-pair offset distribution (each source's clock against a traceable GPS/NTP reference at service or upload events, or from events co-witnessed and independently logged by two sources), the share of contributing sources already traceably synchronised, and a regression-calibration or SIMEX re-fit of a published time-dependence model under that error model reporting the change in per-minute slope, its CI, and the implied benefit of a one-minute improvement. A null settles it equally well.
Novelty — queries run (query → one-line result): 11 searches + 5 fetches at Gate 2; 9 further searches + 4 fetches by adversary 1 in new vocabularies. Full lists: batches/2026-10-17-0742/UQ-20261017-16-record.md and batches/2026-10-17-0742/UQ-20261017-16-adversary-1.md. Most informative: (i) mandatory own-field-own-words query "agreement between dispatch center and defibrillator clock times out-of-hospital cardiac arrest time intervals accuracy" → returned Brabrand 2012 on its first page, i.e. the offset limb already measured; (ii) mandatory "what share of X" query "proportion of hospital medical devices synchronized network time protocol audit clock accuracy survey" → no published fraction; the MD PnP clock-error study is listed as in progress; (iii) "timing error bias estimated per-minute survival decrement OHCA sensitivity analysis mismeasured response interval" → only the slope literature itself, no measurement-error re-fit; (iv) adversary, device-engineering vocabulary, "defibrillator download time stamp aligned with dispatch CAD clock drift correction" → US5749902 (Survivalink, 1996) plus US5921938, US8768441: the offset is a named, patented, corrected-for problem; (v) adversary, standards-body vocabulary, Utstein 2024 template (opened) → core "Response time" is a single-clock dispatch-domain interval. COULD NOT READ: Campbell 1995 full text (paywalled); Goldman's four-hospital clock audit (>1,700 clocks, >1,300 devices — known only via Goodwin's citation, no figures, no DOI located); two PMC-hosted time-to-event measurement-error method papers (not opened, not graded on).
Novelty — nearest prior formulations (3, with sources): PRIOR 1 — Brabrand M et al. "Time telling devices used in Danish health care are not synchronized." Dan Med J 2012;59(10):A4512 (opened in full). Unit: the individual device (11 ED devices, 11 ambulance defibrillators); endpoint: signed offset in mm:ss; reference: NIST/time.gov (±0.2 s); estimand: offset distribution (ED median −00:30, range −17:05 to +01:00; ambulance median −00:45, IQR −02:40 to −00:01), share within 1 min, max inter-device spread 19:05. PRIOR 2 — Srour FJ, Badr NG. "Time Synchronization in Emergency Response Time Measurement." HEALTHINF 2017:199-204, doi 10.5220/0006096001990204 (opened in full). Unit: the call record (24,391, one CAD); endpoint: logically impossible negative intervals; reference: internal ordering only; estimand: error prevalence (89.04%/1.81%/0.77%) and magnitude (medians 70/37/30 s, max 86,400 s). PRIOR 3 — Goodwin AJ et al. "Timing errors and temporal uncertainty in clinical databases: a narrative review." Front Digit Health 2022;4:932599 (opened, publisher route). Unit: the error mechanism; endpoint: taxonomy plus recommendations; no comparator, no estimand; recommends "Employ techniques that incorporate temporal uncertainty into analysis". Supporting: Guo Y, MS thesis, Univ. Washington Biostatistics 2017 — simulated time-to-treatment error biasing a treatment×time interaction in prehospital TBI (record opened). Also real and on-point: US5749902 (Survivalink, filed 1996, opened) — "the response times measured through the AED real time clock often included errors of many minutes", corrected by syncing to the 911 computer clock at download, motivated by the ~10%-per-minute decrement; extended to EMRs by US8768441 (2014).
Novelty — how this differs from each: vs PRIOR 1 — same estimand, same setting, traceable reference, so limb (a) is NOT un-asked; residual differences narrow rather than open it (wall/telephone/defibrillator clocks humans read rather than the systems that write registry stamps; n=22 devices + 11 ambulances, no per-pair distribution, no case linkage; the slope consequence asserted, never estimated). vs PRIOR 2 — within-system error against no external reference, detecting only order-inverting offsets; no outcome model. vs PRIOR 3 — agenda-level statement of the whole question in the adjacent field, ICU/hospital rather than prehospital source set, no offset distribution and no bias analysis of its own. vs Guo — the same statistical manoeuvre one population over, with hypothesised iid error rather than a measured clock-offset model. vs US5749902 — the patent eliminates the offset at download rather than measuring its residual distribution or propagating it to a slope. What remains genuinely undone is only limb (c): the re-fit of a published per-minute decrement under a measured offset model, restricted to intervals that really do cross clocks.
Novelty confidence: Low (unchanged on verification: the Gate 2 ground was re-checked at first hand and survives, while one supporting clause of the adversary's sharpening was refuted and three cited figures were reattributed — see Verification)
Significance — consequence: If multi-clock offsets are material and non-differential, published per-minute decrements are attenuated and the marginal return on a one-minute improvement is understated; if small, the field can retire a caveat recycled since the Utstein report without a number attached. Weakened by the adversary's finding that the slope actually underwriting response-time targets is single-clock, and by documentation latency and bystander collapse-time estimation plausibly dominating clock offset on the intervals that do cross clocks.
Significance — audience: Registry stewards and definition-writing bodies (ILCOR/Utstein, CARES, AHA GWTG, national ambulance regulators); clinical engineering / healthcare technology management (MD PnP); measurement-error methodologists. Real, but already half-mobilised — and that half-mobilisation is itself the prior art.
Significance — fecundity: Makes askable whether offsets are differential by severity through the device-use pathway; whether a traceability requirement changes measured or merely measured-measured performance; whether correction reorders public benchmarking; whether sepsis-bundle and golden-hour slopes inherit the same bias.
Significance — anchoring: The contested stability of the 7-10%-per-minute decrement and the 8-minute target; the Utstein standing complaint that "clock inaccuracy and lack of synchronization continue to be a problem"; Goodwin et al.'s open recommendation.
Reason for silence: Claimed mechanism was a disciplinary boundary (clocks owned by clinical engineering, slopes by resuscitation epidemiology, correction by measurement-error statistics) plus an incentive seam (a registry must label its flagship exposure mismeasured). The mechanism survives for the re-fit only. It does not explain the offset limb, which was asked by device engineers in 1996, patented, and measured in 2012 — so there was no silence there to explain.
Adversarial log (8 rows: attack | objection | response | status): One adversary (fresh context, Gate 0-3 record only, told the Low grade was a prior finding not a verdict); verbatim log in batches/2026-10-17-0742/UQ-20261017-16-adversary-1.md. Disguise WAS executed: 9 new-vocabulary queries against the 8 required, so Disguise is verified, not unverified.
1. Triviality | direction is textbook (Li & Ryan, opened: naive estimates "shrink toward zero"), and Brabrand's IQR against a ~3-4 min response-time SD gives a 10-20% attenuation (adversary's own arithmetic on n=11, so very uncertain) | offsets are device-persistent, sign-coupled across adjacent intervals and time-varying (DST), so the independence Li & Ryan assume fails and the specific number is not page-computable | Partial
2. Disguise | under device-engineering vocabulary the offset limb is named and patented since 1996 (US5749902 "errors of many minutes", corrected at download; US8768441 extends it to EMRs), so limb (a) is a known problem renamed | the composite (measured per-pair offsets + SIMEX re-fit) was not found under any of 9 new vocabularies (EIV/econometrics, device engineering, stroke QI, German, IHCA video-documentation, slope provenance, trauma registry, standards body, registry methods) | Partial
3. Combinatorial novelty | clinical-engineering clock audit × biostatistical error correction, with limb (c) routine once (a) exists; Guo already ran a hypothesised-error version | a real seam problem exists — device-persistent, sign-coupled, possibly outcome-correlated error breaks standard non-differential SIMEX | Partial — plausible but unevidenced that anyone has noticed or that it matters
4. Presupposition failure | presupposition 4 fails for the slope that sets the headline target: Utstein 2024 core "Response time" (opened) is PSAP call-connect → arrival at scene, both dispatch-domain, so inter-source offset cannot bias it; the multi-clock intervals are supplemental and dominated by bystander collapse-time estimation; and sync-at-download since 1996 weakens presupposition 2 | limb (c) can select a multi-clock slope (call-to-first-shock, which also carries targets); Srour & Badr show a single CAD still carries internal synchronisation error; the share synchronised is itself part of the answer | Partial — a restricted version survives, but the candidate does not distinguish single- from multi-clock slopes
5. Vagueness | "attenuate or distort" absorbs any result | the Gate 1 reformulation fixes estimand, reference and source pairs and pre-declares the null informative | Resolved
6. Significance inflation | the "buy ambulances against an understated return" consequence attaches to the immune single-clock slope; for multi-clock intervals direction is known and magnitude likely small; ILCOR's current template (as served) carries no clock-sync statement | audience real; the 1996 patent priced the problem at "many minutes" and Brabrand's ED range shows clocks still wander; an audit figure would be used | Partial — audience real, consequence overstated
7. Reason for silence | the question WAS asked — by Survivalink's engineers in 1996 and by Brabrand in 2012; the silence covers only the re-fit, and epidemiologists plausibly judged clock offset dominated by collapse-time estimation and charting latency | the incentive seam credibly explains why the party with the data has not run the re-fit, and the three literatures demonstrably do not cite each other | Partial
8. Dissolution | offsets are properties of particular devices at particular times, not a stable scientific quantity, so the answer is a site-specific engineering QA report and the re-fit inherits its locality | a multi-site audit with a share-synchronised figure and a slope sensitivity band would still be decision-relevant, as Brabrand's 22-device audit was publishable; a null would generalise | Partial
Verification (post-batch, two fresh-context checkers, logs UQ-20261017-16-verification-utstein.md and -brabrand.md): **the Gate 2 rejection stands, and the sharpening the adversary added to it is REFUTED.** The entry's closing clause held that the slope the question targets — the Utstein core "Response time" — "is written by a single dispatch-domain clock, so inter-source offset cannot bias it at all". The defining documents say otherwise, and they say the opposite of the clause's premise.
**The Utstein clause falls, on the template's own words.** In the 2015 update (Perkins et al.) response time is "The time interval from incoming call to the time the first emergency response vehicle stops"; in the 2024 template (Bray et al.) it is the interval between time point 1, "Time call connects to primary PSAP (recommended)", and time point 2, "Time dispatched first responders or EMS arrived at scene (wheels stop turning; recommended)". So the start is a call-handling event and the end is a **vehicle** event, and neither document says a CAD system records both — a crew or mobile-data-terminal status press, or an AVL/GPS stamp, would be a second clock domain (that mechanism is the checker's inference, labelled as such, not the template's text). The shock-based intervals cross systems unambiguously: call to first defibrillation runs from the same PSAP call to time point 2, "Time of first defibrillation (recommended)". Decisively, the 2015 template names the candidate's own problem and prescribes against it: "The problem of lack of synchronization of clocks and other time-recording devices persists", and "The recommendation remains that 1 clock (or synchronization to a single clock) be used to determine all times". The 2024 template is silent on clocks and instead requires that "A description of all time points used must be included in reporting" and that "This information should be collected from the same source for all cases and documented in reporting". The clause is struck. Note what this does and does not change: it widens the set of intervals the routed slope limb may legitimately address, and it adds the field's own consensus document to the list of places the problem is posed — which if anything *hardens* the asked-but-open finding on the slope limb rather than reviving the candidate. Caveat: the 2015 text was reached only through a secondary copy (a DC Fire and EMS server) because Circulation and Resuscitation could not be opened, and the quotes come from the page summariser, so the wording should be checked against the published version before citation.
**Brabrand's figures are PARTIALLY CONFIRMED, and three of them are misattributed in this entry.** The design is confirmed: each device measured against time.gov on 26 August 2010 at a stated accuracy of ±0.2 s, over 11 devices in the resuscitation rooms of two EDs and 11 ambulance defibrillator watches. But the paper reports ED medians **per hospital**, not pooled: Esbjerg −03:00 (IQR −03:00 to −02:00) and Kolding −00:30 (IQR −08:00 to 00:00). **The −00:30 this entry gives as the ED median is the Kolding figure**; the pooled 11-device median from Table 1 is −02:00. The ambulance median −00:45 and IQR −02:40 to −00:01 do appear in the text, but Table 2 yields a median of −01:26, so **the paper's own text and table disagree** and this entry inherited the text value without the discrepancy. The two "ranges" (−17:05 to +01:00 and −05:22 to +02:00) match the extreme table values but are not printed as ranges. Confirmed as printed: "only two of 11 (18.2%) time telling devices at the emergency departments were running correctly", "the watches deviated less than one minute in only four of 11 defibrillators (36.4%)", and "The maximum deviation between two time telling devices was 19 minutes and five seconds". Also confirmed: the paper reports **no** distribution of pairwise differences, only those two maxima, and links no device to any patient case.
**The "asserts but never estimates" finding is confirmed, and is stronger than the entry claimed.** Verbatim: "the use of unsynchronized time telling devices in research introduces a systematic error", "could lead to skewed results and introduce bias", and "Survival decreases with 7-10% per minute [8] and an error of several minutes in this context could potentially be disastrous." No bias, no survival shift and no effect on any registry estimate is computed anywhere. The checker also surfaced a sentence this entry did not have, which cuts against the prior's own force: "Such a small deviation will probably have little impact on the treatment of our patients or on research." So the nearest prior not only declines to estimate the consequence, it dismisses it in passing — which makes the slope limb more clearly asked-and-unanswered, not less, and is the strongest available support for the routed row.
**Where it lands. Rejected, unchanged, on the ground that survives.** The Gate 2 kill never rested on the Utstein clause: it rests on the offset limb having been asked, patented and corrected for in 1996 (US5749902) and measured against a traceable reference in this very setting in 2012 (Brabrand), with the slope limb named as an explicit open recommendation by Goodwin et al. 2022. Verification touches none of that. What it changes is the entry's accuracy: one supporting clause is struck, three figures are reattributed, and the routed row gains a better source. Caveat: Brabrand was read through the summariser and a direct PDF fetch returned HTTP 403, so the Table 2 median mismatch should be re-checked against the PDF before anyone cites either median.

Scores: Well-posedness 3/3 · Significance 2/3
Strongest remaining objection: The offset limb that carries the question's empirical content was asked, patented and corrected for in 1996 (US5749902) and measured against a traceable NIST reference in this very setting in 2012 (Brabrand), while the slope limb was stated as an explicit open recommendation by Goodwin et al. 2022 — so the candidate is a disguised known bolted to an asked-but-unanswered analysis, not an un-asked question; The clause that previously closed this objection — that the Utstein core "Response time" is written by a single dispatch-domain clock, so inter-source offset cannot bias it — is WITHDRAWN on verification: the 2024 template runs that interval from a PSAP call-connect event to a vehicle-stop event and names no recording system, and the 2015 update states that "The problem of lack of synchronization of clocks and other time-recording devices persists". The withdrawal widens the set of intervals the routed limb may address; it does not disturb the Gate 2 ground above.
Suggested first step toward an answer (pointer only — do not take it): For the routed slope limb, first settle which published per-minute models are fitted on genuinely multi-clock intervals by reading their methods sections, then bound the attenuation from Brabrand's published offset distribution before any new data collection.
Routing (if rejected as already-asked): Limb (a) is NOT routed — it is answered at device level (Brabrand 2012) and engineered around (US5749902), i.e. a disguised known. Limb (c) IS routed to ledger/routed-open-problems.md as an asked-but-unanswered quantitative-bias analysis, restricted to genuinely multi-clock intervals (call-to-first-shock: CAD × defibrillator; EMS-to-ED hand-off: ePCR × ED triage). Row: | 2026-10-17 | UQ-20261017-16 | Re-fit a published per-minute outcome-vs-elapsed-time decrement for a genuinely multi-clock prehospital interval (call-to-first-shock, EMS-to-ED hand-off) under a measured inter-source clock-offset error model by regression calibration or SIMEX, reporting the change in slope, CI and implied benefit of a one-minute improvement. Posed in print as a consequence and as a recommendation; never estimated. | Brabrand et al., Dan Med J 2012;59(10):A4512 — "the use of unsynchronized time telling devices in research introduces a systematic error and could lead to skewed results", alongside "Survival decreases with 7-10% per minute": consequence asserted, never estimated; Goodwin et al., Front Digit Health 2022;4:932599, doi 10.3389/fdgth.2022.932599 — "Employ techniques that incorporate temporal uncertainty into analysis", recommended, never applied to a per-minute decrement | B (a bounded sensitivity band is computable from Brabrand's published offset distribution plus a published slope and exposure SD; a true re-fit needs registry case-level timestamps and a measured per-pair offset model, nearer C) | |

ID: UQ-20261017-17
Date: 2026-10-17
Status: Provisional
Domain(s): Medicine — acute pain management and analgesic-trial methodology (target field). Adjacent: PRO psychometrics (response shift, longitudinal measurement invariance); health econometrics (reporting heterogeneity); psychophysics (range–frequency context effects).

Question (canonical): In adult inpatients with an acute pain episode scored serially for >= 48 h, with a then-test at a randomly assigned day and a pre-registered external anchor set (opioid-equivalent consumption/PCA demands, QST, a functional milestone such as time to first ambulation): (a) does a longitudinal measurement-invariance model of the serial 0–10 NRS, anchors as reference, reject intercept (scalar) invariance across the episode; (b) under a pre-declared operationalisation of recalibration (then-test difference, or fitted intercept drift), what fraction of the mean observed within-episode NRS reduction is recalibration rather than change in anchored pain; and (c) at the NRS <= 4 titration target and the 2-point/30% MCID, what misclassification rate of "target attained"/"MCID achieved" does that recalibration induce? Both estimates must be shown not to be recall error, via randomised then-test timing and an anchor-only refit.
(V2; the single Gate 1 reformulation, spent to pin population, operationalisation, anchor set and estimands. V1 and full text in batches/2026-10-17-0742/UQ-20261017-17-record.md.)

Alternative formulations:
- When a post-operative patient's score falls from 8 to 4 over two days, how much of the fall is the pain changing and how much is the patient's internal "10" changing?
- Is the acute-pain NRS longitudinally invariant over hours to days within one episode, and if not, what bias does that put into NRS-change endpoints and into protocols that titrate opioids to a fixed NRS threshold?

Motivating gap:
Source method: presupposition inversion. The inverted settled claim is that a falling NRS means improving pain, which presupposes a fixed sensation-to-number mapping over the episode. Recalibration response shift is established for bodily pain in surgical patients at the 3-month scale (P1) and is large and common in surgical PROMs at 1–2 years (P2), but has not been examined on the hours-to-days timescale, on the single-item NRS, or with a dosing decision attached to the number. Two adjacent findings sharpen rather than close the gap: the acute field ran a 2,661-patient serial-PROM study in exactly this window and asked only responsiveness (PROMPT NIT-1, BJA 2024; median sensitivity-to-change 0.22), and it has documented cross-sectional misclassification by a fixed NRS cut-off (P3: 17% over-/5% under-treatment at NRS > 4). Neither asks whether the scale itself moves during the episode.

Presuppositions:
1. Experienced pain and its rating are separable in principle. CONTESTED; principal dissolution risk. Mitigated, not removed, by declaring the estimand anchor-relative.
2. A then-test (or equivalent invariance model) can distinguish recalibration from recall error. CONTESTED; hence randomised then-test timing plus anchor-only refit.
3. A non-recalibrating anchor exists over the episode. CONTESTED — and the gate-limiting item: see Strongest remaining objection.
4. The NRS is used as if interval-scaled with stable anchoring in titration protocols and trial endpoints. ESTABLISHED.
5. Episodes with >= 24–72 h of serial scoring are common. ESTABLISHED (routine 4-hourly charting).
6. A then-test rating is obtainable without the clinical context cueing a socially desirable answer. CONTESTED — and now evidenced against: van Dijk 2016, Bosdet 2021 (below).
7. (Gate 1) Floor/ceiling and the "worst pain imaginable" anchor do not themselves produce the whole effect; a mechanism of recalibration, but modelled separately.

What would count as an answer:
A within-episode then-test plus a longitudinal invariance analysis of serial NRS against a pre-registered external anchor: a recalibration share of observed NRS change, under at least two pre-declared operationalisations, plus the misclassification rate of "titration target attained" and "MCID achieved". The estimate must be shown not to be recall error by design (randomised then-test timing; anchor-only refit). A null — scalar invariance holds within the episode — is a clean answer and retires the concern for both titration protocols and NRS-change endpoints.

Novelty — queries run (query → one-line result):
Gate 2: 11 web searches, 4 fetches (cap-limited); Gate 4: 18 further NEW-vocabulary queries (9 per adversary) and 8 fetches. Full lists in batches/2026-10-17-0742/UQ-20261017-17-record.md and in UQ-20261017-17-adversary-1.md / -adversary-2.md. Most informative:
- (own-field obvious title) "response shift" in postoperative pain intensity / do serial pain scores measure the same construct over time → nearest hit PROMPT NIT-1, BJA 2024 (opened): responsiveness at days 1/3/7, n=2,661, median sensitivity-to-change 0.22; measures responsiveness, not invariance.
- (fraction limb — already computed?) proportion of observed pain-score change attributable to recalibration → the nearest published figure anywhere is P1's "recalibration added 4.4% to the total 29.8% explained variance of bodily pain" at 3 months, which verification confirms is incremental explained variance and not a share of change at all, so no published share exists. No within-episode share, no published misclassification rate of NRS-target attainment under recalibration.
- (searching for the answer to limb (c)) validity of titrating analgesia to NRS < 4, misclassification → P3 (opened): cross-sectional NRS-vs-VRS mismatch, 17%/5% at NRS > 4.
- (method-owning field) time-varying measurement non-invariance in intensive longitudinal data, single-item self-report → method family mature in psychometrics/ILD; no application to serial acute-pain NRS.
- (Gate 4, psychophysics — the miss Gate 2 made) "adaptation level" OR "range-frequency" context effects pain rating scale internal standard → Watkinson et al., Pain 2013;154(5):743-749 (P4 below), found independently by both adversaries.
- (Gate 4, qualitative nursing) how patients use the 0–10 scale, frame of reference, interviews → van Dijk et al., Int J Nurs Stud 2016;53:260-269 (opened) and Bosdet et al., Front Pain Res 2021;2 (opened): patients set the reported number partly on anticipated analgesic administration and staff judgement; both single-timepoint.
- (Gate 4, health econometrics pre-vignette vocabulary) "scale of reference bias" OR "state-dependent reporting bias" self-reported pain → Groot, J Health Econ 2000; Eur J Health Econ 2003: same construct, QoL object, population timescale.
- (Gate 4) SDT criterion-vs-discriminability; IRT item-parameter drift / longitudinal DIF for pain items; German-language Rekalibrierung Schmerzskala; burns repeated-dressing ratings → method vocabularies alive, none applied to within-episode acute NRS.
Negative recorded in both the data-owning and the method-owning vocabularies, on 29 queries and 12 opened/partially-opened sources — not on absence in one vocabulary.

Novelty — nearest prior formulations (3, with sources):
P1. Visser MRM, Oort FJ, van Lanschot JJB, et al. "The role of recalibration response shift in explaining bodily pain in cancer patients undergoing invasive surgery." Psycho-Oncology 2013;22(3):515-522. doi 10.1002/pon.2114. PARTIAL READ (pure.eur.nl institutional record; publisher full text COULD NOT READ — generator out of fetch budget, adversary #1 got HTTP 429 at doi.org with an instruction not to retry). Unit: patient (N=202), one pre/post pair. Endpoint: multi-item bodily-pain QoL subscale. Reference: then-test (pretest minus then-test). Estimand: incremental explained variance from recalibration, 4.4% of a total 29.8%, over pre-surgery to 3 months. Two further attempts on verification also failed to open the publisher full text (Wiley errored twice, three repository records gave abstract level only, Europe PMC robots-disallowed), so everything here is abstract level; the pain instrument is named only as a construct in every record opened.
P2. Marmura H, Getgood A, Bryant DM. "Does Response Shift Theory Explain Why We Are Underestimating Treatment Effects In PROs Following ACL Reconstruction?" ISAKOS 2025 abstract 19760 (abstract opened; no journal full text located). Unit: patient (171 ACLR). Endpoint: KOOS/IKDC, multi-item 0–100, with then-test versions. Reference: then-test-adjusted vs unadjusted change. Estimand: adjusted-minus-unadjusted change (3–18 points) and prevalence of >= 10-point recalibration (~75%/78% at 1/2 y). Pain-subscale-specific figure NOT confirmed; not graded on.
P3. van Dijk JFM, van Wijck AJM, Kappen TH, et al. "Postoperative pain assessment based on numeric ratings is not the same for patients and professionals." Int J Nurs Stud 2012;49(1):65-71. Full text opened (Utrecht DSpace). Unit: NRS–VRS response pair (n=10,434) and clinician (~303). Endpoint: NRS-VRS correspondence, bearability. Reference: patient's own VRS. Estimand: misclassification of fixed NRS cut-offs at one time point, ~24 h post-op (17%/5% at NRS > 4); explicitly does not measure analgesic use.
P4 (added at Gate 4 — found independently by both adversaries, missed by Gate 2). Watkinson P, Wood AM, Lloyd DM, Brown GDA. "Pain ratings reflect cognitive context: a range frequency model of pain perception." Pain 2013;154(5):743-749. doi 10.1016/j.pain.2013.01.016. PARTIAL READ (Leeds Trinity and Warwick repository records; publisher full text not obtained, so the participant population is inferred, not confirmed). Unit: a rated stimulus within one laboratory session. Endpoint: 0–10 rating of pressure pain. Reference: between-subject stimulus distribution. Estimand: dependence of the rating on the rank/range of its context — "pain ratings are relative to the surrounding context". Three independent attempts across thirteen fetches failed to obtain the full text (PMID 23498366; Semantic Scholar reports no open-access PDF), so this grade rests on repository abstract summaries, which support a between-subject context effect and not within-person temporal drift (see Verification).
Near-miss, opened: PROMPT NIT-1, Br J Anaesth 2024;132(1):96-106 — candidate's exact window and population, anchor items used, but estimand is responsiveness, which presupposes rather than tests scale stability.

Novelty — how this differs from each:
- vs P1: unit matches; endpoint (multi-item QoL subscale vs single-item NRS charted 4-hourly), reference (3-month pre/post then-test with no external anchor vs within-episode randomised-timing then-test against a pre-registered anchor set plus anchor-only refit) and estimand (incremental SEM variance vs share of observed change and decision misclassification) all differ. P1 establishes the construct at the month scale; it caps novelty at Medium.
- vs P2: endpoint again multi-item 0–100 knee PROMs; timescale 1–2 years post-discharge; reference a single recalled pre-operative state, not serial within-episode measurement; estimand a points-shift and per-patient prevalence, not a share of change or a threshold misclassification rate.
- vs P3: closest prior on limb (c) and the only published NRS misclassification percentages found, but the estimand is cross-sectional between-rater disagreement about what a number means at one instant, not within-patient drift in the number's meaning over an episode; deliberately unlinked to analgesic administration.
- vs P4: same response scale and the same relativity claim, which is why it does real damage to limb (a) — but unit is a laboratory stimulus in a single session, reference is a between-subject stimulus distribution, and there is no clinical episode, no anchor set, no share of observed change and no decision threshold. It bounds the candidate's conceptual novelty to zero and leaves its estimand novelty intact.

Novelty confidence: Medium (bottom of range)
Two close neighbours, not one: P1 on the construct in the same patient population, P4 on the identical 0–10 pain response in the candidate's own flagship journal. Not Low: across 29 queries and 12 sources no prior matches the candidate's unit–endpoint–reference–estimand combination; limb (b)'s quantity appears nowhere and limb (c)'s nearest published number (P3) answers a different question. Not a disguised known on the judge's reading: both adversaries ran full Disguise sweeps in new vocabularies and neither produced a renamed version — the candidate is an estimand transposition with an interface-specific object (limb (c)), not a pure instrument/timescale swap. But it is a transposition of a live research programme, not a new concept, and the record's "scale stability never questioned" claim is false as stated now that P4 is on the table.

Significance — consequence:
If yes and the share is material, two things read as measurements become partly measurements of the instrument. (i) NRS-change endpoints in acute analgesic trials carry a bias whose sign depends on whether recalibration runs with or against true improvement; if common to both arms it attenuates contrasts and would partly explain PROMPT NIT-1's median sensitivity-to-change of 0.22, and if it differs by arm (plausible where arms differ in opioid exposure or in severe-pain experience) it biases the treatment effect. Note P4's range–frequency prediction runs the other way for early scores, so the sign is not derivable a priori. (ii) Protocols titrating opioids to a fixed threshold would be acting on a moving target — a direct opioid-stewardship consequence. If no (scalar invariance holds), the concern is retired for both uses and the response-shift literature's reach into acute endpoints is bounded.

Significance — audience:
Acute pain services and authors of inpatient pain-assessment/opioid-titration protocols; acute analgesic-trial methodologists and core-outcome groups (IMMPACT/ACTTION, the PROMPT/standardised-endpoint collaborations); regulators assessing acute analgesic endpoints; the response-shift/PRO psychometrics community. Specifiable actions: add an anchor or then-test to the acute protocol, re-derive the MCID on an invariance-corrected scale, add an anchored co-primary endpoint, or stop worrying. Adversary #2's counter stands partly: P3 published a cleaner, non-anchor-relative indictment of the NRS > 4 threshold fourteen years ago and the convention persists, so the trial-methodology audience is the more responsive one and the opioid-stewardship consequence is the weakest limb of the case.

Significance — fecundity:
Opens whether anchored/calibrated acute scales (vignette-anchored, QST-referenced, forced-choice) track change better than the free NRS; whether the 2-point/30% MCID is partly a recalibration artefact; whether recalibration is itself a worthwhile treatment effect rather than a bias; whether it differs by opioid exposure, by whether the index event reset the patient's worst-ever pain, and by first vs repeat episode; and whether the same drift affects the other bedside single-item scales on the same cadence (dyspnoea, nausea, sedation).

Significance — anchoring:
Three standing anomalies rather than an invented one: the documented mismatch between NRS thresholds and patients' own bearability (P3); the unexplained low sensitivity-to-change of acute postsurgical PROMs in a large multicentre study (PROMPT NIT-1); and the open methodological dispute over whether then-test recalibration estimates are recall artefacts, which a short-recall design would inform.

Reason for silence:
Disciplinary boundary — the surviving mechanism, and acceptable on Gate 4's list. The method family (then-test designs, scalar-invariance SEM, intensive-longitudinal invariance) is owned by HRQoL/psycho-oncology and ILD methodology and presumes a research-visit cadence; the pain field's own scale-usage work reached for psychophysics and range–frequency theory (P4) and for qualitative interviews (van Dijk 2016, Bosdet 2021) and never for invariance machinery. Both adversaries' sweeps show this split directly: measurement vocabularies alive but unapplied to pain, pain vocabularies alive but cross-sectional.
Two mechanisms the record offered FAIL and are struck. (ii) Incentive/taboo: contradicted by direct evidence — the pain and nursing literature publishes exactly the doubt that patients' numbers are not stimulus-faithful, aimed at the patient (van Dijk 2016: the reported number is weighed against anticipated analgesic administration and staff judgement; Bosdet 2021: idiosyncratic grounding of the same words; Pain itself published P4). (iii) Data/instrument: weak — 4-hourly charting is routine by presupposition 5 and a then-test is one extra question. Per Gate 4's own instruction, two of three mechanisms failing weakens rather than supports the novelty finding; it does not overturn a Medium grade that no duplicate was found against.

Verification (post-batch, four fresh-context checkers, logs UQ-20261017-17-verification-adaptation.md, -visser.md, -watkinson.md and -watkinson2.md): **Provisional stands untouched, because nothing verification reached bears on the objection that holds it there — but one promotion condition is discharged in the candidate's favour, and two of this entry's own claims are overstated.**
**The Disguise negative's one unrun read has now been run, and it is off point.** "Anticipated adaptation or scale recalibration?", the PMC4016565 item Gate 4 recorded as an unrun read rather than a check that passed, was reached at the publisher (hqlo.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/1477-7525-11-171, after PMC returned a captcha and Europe PMC was robots-disallowed) and is Edelaar-Peeters & Stiggelbout, Health Qual Life Outcomes 2013;11:171. It studies 44 spinal-cord-injury patients rating health on a 100 mm VAS anchored death to perfect health and in time trade-off, at admission, discharge and after discharge — months apart, not within an episode — and it reports no share of change, no threshold or MCID, and no pain instrument at all; its tentative conclusion separates accurate anticipation (TTO) from recalibration (VAS). CONFIRMED not on point. So the Rejection branch this entry reserved for it does not fire, and that half of the promotion condition is discharged.
**P4's pre-answering of limb (a) is overstated, and P4 was never read.** Two further checkers spent thirteen fetch attempts between them and every route failed: doi.org client error, ScienceDirect robots-disallowed on a guessed PII, Europe PMC robots-disallowed, a guessed journals.lww.com URL in error, PubMed returning a captcha twice, Warwick WRAP restricted with no PDF, Stirling embargoed to 3000-01-01 behind request-a-copy, Leeds Trinity advertising CC BY but linking only the DOI, the one permitted PMC attempt robots-disallowed, and the Semantic Scholar API confirming no open-access PDF while supplying PMID 23498366. The Oxford WIN record that surfaces on a title search is a different 2019 J Pain paper (hierarchical drift diffusion, N=37) and must not be mistaken for it. What the abstract supports, through repository summaries rather than verbatim text: participants rated three blocks of 11 pressure pain stimuli on a 0–10 scale with the stimulus distribution varied BETWEEN participants; Study 1 found a stimulus rated higher when it ranked highest within its context; Study 2 found ratings higher when most stimuli were relatively intense with mean intensity held constant. That is a context or stimulus-set effect, and it is NOT a demonstration that one person's mapping from sensation onto the number drifts over time across an episode. Whether the body reports any within-person block or time effect is unknown, not absent. So this entry's "limb (a) is largely pre-answered" — attack 1, repeated in the second-strongest objection — carries more than its source supports: P4 shows the rating depends on its company, which is why novelty sits at the Medium floor, but the temporal-drift claim limb (a) makes is in nothing that was read. What survives intact is the narrower charge the same objection makes, that the record's "scale stability never questioned" line is false as written, because P4 questions it.
**P1's 4.4% is not a share of change, and that cuts in the candidate's favour.** The Visser full text could not be opened either (Wiley errored twice, three repository records gave abstract level only, Europe PMC robots-disallowed). Confirmed at abstract level: N=202, before surgery and three months after, a then-test design with response shift as pretest minus then-test bodily pain, SEM followed by sequential regression, RMSEA 0.03 (90% CI 0.000–0.071), chi-square(18)=21.13, p=.27, and "Recalibration response shift had a unique albeit small contribution to the explanation of bodily pain." Decisively for this entry: the 4.4% is incremental explained variance added to a total of 29.8%, not a proportion of observed change. This entry called it "the only published share anywhere" and attack 6 called it "the one comparable magnitude"; neither holds, and the corrected statement is stronger for the candidate, since no published share of change exists at all. Also not found in any record opened: the name of the pain instrument, which the abstract gives only as a construct, and its item count.
**Where it lands. Provisional, unchanged.** The objection that caps this entry is that no anchor is invariant by construction, so limb (b) estimates recalibration plus strategic reporting plus anchor drift. It rests on van Dijk et al. 2016 and Bosdet et al. 2021, both of which the batch opened at first hand, and verification touched neither; well-posedness stays 2/3. The net of the four checks is an entry that is more accurate and slightly better placed than it was: one promotion condition discharged, the comparator magnitude corrected in the candidate's favour, and the strongest pre-answering claim against it withdrawn to what its source actually supports.

Scores: Well-posedness 2/3 · Significance 2/3

Strongest remaining objection:
The anchor set cannot do the work the question needs, so limb (b) is not identified. Both adversaries converged on this independently: van Dijk et al. 2016 (Int J Nurs Stud 53:260-269, opened) finds patients fix the number they report partly on anticipated analgesic administration and on how staff will judge them, and Bosdet et al. 2021 (Front Pain Res 2;2, opened) finds the scale is "frequently used to request pain medication" — so the lead anchor (PCA demands / opioid consumption) and the reported NRS are two outputs of one wish-for-analgesia process, QST measures evoked rather than clinical pain, and time-to-ambulation is protocol-driven. With no anchor invariant by construction, "scale drift" and "anchor drift" are not separable from the data, and V2's two safeguards (randomised then-test timing, anchor-only refit) address recall and then-test dependence but not strategic reporting, which shares recalibration's signature. What limb (b) estimates is recalibration + strategic reporting + anchor drift, not recalibration. (Second strongest, as corrected on verification: P4 shows the rating of a fixed stimulus depends on the distribution of stimuli it sits among, on the identical 0–10 scale, and its omission makes the record's "scale stability never questioned" claim false as written — but P4's full text was never obtained and its abstract supports a between-subject context effect, not the within-person temporal drift limb (a) asserts, so "largely pre-answers limb (a)" is withdrawn as overstated.)

Promotion requires: re-scoring well-posedness to 3/3 on new evidence — specifically, published evidence that at least one pre-declared anchor is plausibly invariant over 48 h and is not a shared output of the wish-for-analgesia process (or a design element that identifies recalibration against strategic reporting, e.g. then-test administration independent of the treating team) . The second half of this condition is partly discharged on verification: PMC4016565 was opened at the publisher, identified as Edelaar-Peeters & Stiggelbout, Health Qual Life Outcomes 2013;11:171, and confirmed off point, so the Rejection branch this entry reserved for it does not fire; P4 (Watkinson 2013) and P1 (Visser 2013) remain unread in full after two further independent attempts each and still bear on the Disguise grade. Absent the well-posedness evidence the entry stays Provisional however those two reads come back.

Suggested first step toward an answer (pointer only — do not take it):
Pointer only: the archival half of this step is done — PMC4016565 was opened by publisher route on verification and is off point — so what remains is to obtain P4 and P1 in full by a route a repository can satisfy (each resisted five independent fetch attempts), and to ask the method-owning literature (intensive-longitudinal measurement invariance) what it requires of a reference indicator when the candidate references are treatment-affected. If none qualifies, the live question is limb (c) alone, which needs no anchored decomposition.

Routing (if rejected as already-asked): n/a — not rejected.

ID: UQ-20261017-18
Date: 2026-10-17
Status: Rejected
Domain(s): Medicine — health-systems quality measurement and payment policy (target field; CMS/NCQA/HQIP measure and audit programmes would act). Method transplanted from election auditing / statistical audit sampling (risk-limiting audits).
Question (canonical): For a named threshold-linked hospital quality measure whose data elements come from human chart abstraction or discretionary clinician entry (e.g. a CMS IQR chart-abstracted measure such as SEP-1), and taking as the audit target the result of complete re-abstraction of all eligible charts rather than "truth": (a) does there exist a sequential re-abstraction sampling-and-stopping rule which, under a pre-registered bounded-per-case abstraction-error model, guarantees that the probability of stopping without escalating to complete re-abstraction, when complete re-abstraction WOULD reverse the hospital's payment or rating classification, is at most alpha; and (b) applying such a rule to a real hospital cohort, in what fraction of hospitals does confirmation of the reported classification at alpha = 0.05 require re-abstracting more than a pre-stated share (say 50%) of eligible charts?
Alternative formulations: (1) As intake (V1, retained in the record): what sequential re-abstraction sample would bound, at a stated risk limit, the probability that complete re-abstraction would move a hospital across its payment or rating threshold, and across a cohort, in what fraction is the reported margin to threshold smaller than documented abstraction disagreement implies? (2) How often is a hospital's penalty or rating an artefact of abstraction error rather than of care? (recorded as the weaker phrasing: it reintroduces the contested truth standard that V2 removes). The canonical above is the one Gate 1 reformulation, retained in full in the record.
Motivating gap: As submitted — threshold misclassification of hospitals has been quantified only for SAMPLING noise (Shen, Wadhera, Yeh, JAMA Cardiol 2021;6(3):332-335: 10.1-20.9% misclassified penalty status, "up to 31%", cause stated as "a point estimate with a margin of error"), while existing validation audits sample a small fixed number of charts and report element agreement — a data-accuracy statistic about the hospital, not a bound on the decision. FALSIFIED AT GATE 4 in its load-bearing half: abstraction/coding disagreement HAS been propagated to hospital threshold and pay-for-performance decisions across a cohort (Haviari et al. 2019, below). The programme-description half SURVIVES and was verified at Gate 4: CMS IQR validation is fixed-n (up to eight cases per quarter per hospital), scored at measure level, pass at "the upper bound of the confidence interval is 75% or higher", with no provision for expanding the sample and no link to the hospital's measure rate or any payment threshold (FY27 validation webinar, opened); HQIP outlier guidance escalates on a 10/5/25/20-working-day calendar and asks at Stage 4 whether the data "contained inaccuracies" with no method, sample size or risk limit (opened at Gate 2).
Presuppositions: (1) Threshold-linked measures with abstraction-dependent elements feed a payment or rating decision — ESTABLISHED, but must be scoped to abstraction-dependent measures (much of HRRP/HVBP is claims-based). (2) Expert re-abstraction is closer to truth — CONTESTED, DISSOLVED by the canonical form, which targets the full re-abstraction result. (3) Element-level disagreement rates are published or estimable — ESTABLISHED (Garza 2022: all-field 1.24% [1.14, 1.34], populated-field 3.04% [2.81, 3.30]; Illinois APORS per-field accuracy 80.9-96.7%). (4) The decision is a threshold or rank crossing so a margin is well defined — ESTABLISHED for penalty programmes, CONTESTED for composite star ratings; and FURTHER WEAKENED at Gate 4, which notes HVBP/HRRP payment is a continuous function of the score (adversary's recalled claim, NOT verified, so it grounds nothing). (5) Abstraction error is representable as a bounded per-case perturbation — the record calls this CONTESTED and part of the question; Gate 4 shows it is UNCONTESTED for additive measures such as SEP-1 (one chart moves the numerator by at most one case) and contested only for shrunken risk-standardised ones, so the record overstates it. (6) Re-abstraction to the required depth is feasible — CONTESTED, part of limb (b).
What would count as an answer: (i) A stated-risk audit procedure for at least one real threshold-linked abstraction-dependent measure — explicit abstraction-error model, derived sequential sampling and stopping rule with escalation to complete re-abstraction, validated by simulation on real re-abstraction data showing realised risk <= nominal alpha. (ii) An empirical margin-versus-error analysis: the fraction of hospitals whose classification cannot be confirmed at alpha = 0.05 without near-complete re-abstraction. "Almost all are confirmable from a small sample" vindicates cheap fixed-n validation; "many are not" makes it unfit for its decisions; "no margin statistic exists for shrunken model-based measures" is admissible and would be the most consequential.

Most informative: (i) mandatory own-field-own-words query "effect of chart abstraction error on hospital quality measure performance and pay-for-performance penalty status" → vendor and SEP-1-variability pieces only, no abstraction-error-to-penalty link — i.e. the query that SHOULD have found the prior and did not, because it searched "abstraction" rather than "coding"; (ii) mandatory "what fraction of X" query "proportion of hospitals misclassified public reporting abstraction error reabstraction disagreement" → reported NO published figure; DEFEATED at Gate 4; (iii) "\"risk-limiting audit\" clinical quality measure medical record re-abstraction hospital" → no RLA in healthcare at all; (iv) adversary, clinical-coding/registry-audit vocabulary, "data audit validation changed risk-adjusted mortality outlier status hospital reclassification registry re-abstraction impact on performance ranking" → Haviari et al. 2019 on the first page (OPENED, publisher route); (v) adversary, finite-population sequential-testing vocabulary, "sequential probability ratio test finite population hypergeometric proportion exceeds threshold stopping rule record audit misclassified records" → Kato & Nakagawa, arXiv:2604.06116v2 (OPENED), the item the record flagged as "THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT UNREAD ITEM"; (vi) adversary verification query on the CMS IQR validation design → FY27 webinar opened, confirming the record's recalled description; (vii) adversary, German external-QA vocabulary (IQTIG Datenvalidierung) → fixed sample of up to 20 cases per hospital, escalation on an error-rate confidence bound, sample size independent of distance from the Referenzbereich: adjacent, not prior.
