Promotion item (1) is substantially DISCHARGED and novelty is stronger for it; item (2) is UNVERIFIED and ill-formed as written, and is reworded below; item (3) is unchanged.
V1. Item (1) EXECUTED: three of its four named targets opened, one unreadable, and no prior found that plots a clinical ICS endpoint against an individually determined delivered dose. The Chrystyn vocabulary crossed with clinical outcomes (3 searches) returned no such study; the one Chrystyn paper opened, Chrystyn & Milton-Edwards 2025 (J Aerosol Med Pulm Drug Deliv, doi 10.1089/jamp.2024.0063), uses inhaled VOLUME in litres as its sensor variable against exacerbation prediction (ROC-AUC 0.77 COPD n = 336; 0.83 asthma n = 360), ACT and FEV1 (r = 0.609, n = 100), and reports no emitted dose and no dose-response. The Dundee thesis is Anderson WJ, MD 2016, "Personalising Inhaled Corticosteroid Dose Response in Persistent Asthma" (Lipworth and Fardon supervising): landing page opened, thesis body not; "personalising" there means phenotype and biomarker personalisation of the response to a PRESCRIBED dose, and its companion paper (Anderson, Short, Jabbal & Lipworth, Ann Allergy Asthma Immunol 2017;118(2):179-185, author PDF opened) pools four RCTs and 121 evaluable adults on a nominal BDP-equivalent axis — FEV1 +3.3% (95% CI 2.0 to 4.7, about 98 ml) plateauing from 200 to 800 ug while FeNO (40.4 to 26.8 to 20.8 ppb) and AHR (1.35 doubling dilutions) keep moving, i.e. endpoint-dependent curve shape on the LABEL-dose axis with no delivered dose anywhere. The Mouksassi PAGE 21 (2012) Abstr 2480 names between-subject, relative-potency and within-subject/residual variability and does NOT include delivered-dose dispersion. Bentham 10.2174/157488507779422392 is identified from Crossref as Selroos O, "Some Aspects on Comparative Efficacy Studies with Inhaled Corticosteroids in Asthma", Current Drug Therapy 2007, and is COULD NOT READ (publisher routes errored, no abstract in the metadata), so it grades nothing in either direction and is the one piece of item (1) left open.
V2. The two titles-only leads that survey surfaced on the delivered-dose side are now OPENED, and neither is a prior on the clinical limb. The "Bradford emitted dose" lead is THE SAME PAPER as this entry's nearest prior — Tarsin/Assi/Pearson/Chrystyn, Int J Pharm 2006;316:131-137, doi 10.1016/j.ijpharm.2006.02.040, with author order differing between the Bradford and Huddersfield repository records — not a new source, and still abstract-level after six further fetches (publisher errored; both repository PDFs closed or restricted). Its abstract's only analysis is fine particle dose against PIFR: linear for all four drugs (p < 0.001) with slopes about 3x steeper for budesonide (p = 0.002) and 2.8x for formoterol (p = 0.007) — a device-dependence finding, with no clinical outcome and no severity-dose relationship. Hamilton M, Leggett R, Pang C, Charles S, Gillett B, Prime D, J Aerosol Med Pulm Drug Deliv 2015;28(6):498-506, doi 10.1089/jamp.2015.1225, read as full text, is purely in vitro: ELLIPTA with the eLung, an oropharyngeal throat cast and an NGI at a constant 60 l/min, five profiles per therapy chosen as the PIFR minimum, maximum, median and interquartile points rather than as a patient sample, each run in triplicate; it reports a mean with a range per profile and NO SD or CV across profiles (the data were "not large enough to perform formal statistical analysis"), and no clinical outcome is measured or related to per-profile dose. The limb therefore stays unoccupied.
V3. Item (2) is UNVERIFIED — the check ran, the answer did not arrive — so it caps at Provisional and does not reject. One source was opened: STORM (J Aerosol Med Pulm Drug Deliv 2022, doi 10.1089/jamp.2021.0046), extrafine BDP/FF/GB pMDI, 9 asthma and 10 healthy subjects, intrapulmonary deposition 25.50% +/- 6.81% of the nominal dose, a CV of about 26.7% derived by the reader and not published. De Backer 2010, the NEXThaler study, two budesonide device studies and Newman 2000 are unread, with four routes failed (ERJ server error, PMC blocked, ScienceDirect robots, and a 429 telling the reader not to retry). One extrafine formulation at n = 9 is not the imaging answer the condition asks for, and extrafine particles are selected for uniform deposition, so it cannot settle the condition in either direction.
V4. Item (2) is also ILL-FORMED as written, which verification established rather than discharged. The "24-56%" band is NOT a published range: it is derived by a reader from the four mean (SD) pairs of fine particle dose as % label claim in Assi/Tarsin 2006 alone — fluticasone 20.4 (4.8) = CV 23.5%, salmeterol 18.4 (4.4) = 23.9%, budesonide 23.1 (12.9) = 55.8%, formoterol 20.7 (11.1) = 53.6%, at label doses 500, 50, 200 and 6 ug — so it mixes two drugs and two devices in one cohort of 20 severe asthmatics, and it is a DEVICE-EXIT measurand. Setting it against an intrapulmonary-deposition CV, as the condition instructed, compares two different measurands, which is why STORM's 26.7% sitting at the bottom of the band settles nothing. Assi is read at ABSTRACT level only, and its measurement is explicitly ex vivo ("Using an ex vivo method, the Electronic Lung...") on profiles recorded from "20 severe asthmatics (mean PEFR 53% predicted)", with no clinical endpoint anywhere in it; both facts are recorded against the entry's use of it.
V5. Masoli 2004 (Clin Rev Allergy Immunol 4(2):144-148) is COULD NOT READ after six routes (doi.org, two Springer routes, a PubMed page behind reCAPTCHA, a Crossref 429, and Semantic Scholar reporting openAccessPdf CLOSED). Nothing is inferred from it; it grades nothing.
V6. One new datum on the severity-interaction limb, which previously had none: STORM reports "no significant correlations between drug deposition and any of the baseline lung function parameters", with no coefficients given, in 9 asthma patients. That is weak first evidence against the interaction this question needs, recorded as such and not as a settled answer.
Scores: Well-posedness 2/3 · Significance 2/3
Well-posedness loses its third point twice over: the mechanism had to be re-specified before the question was answerable at all (an analyst reading V1 would run a classical-error correction on Berkson-structured data), and identifiability is only conditional — (a) and (c) separate only given an independent per-patient delivery measurement whose validity is the live IVIVC dispute, and whose stated estimator measures emitted rather than deposited dose. Significance holds at 2: the audience is specific and blocked on exactly this, both branches move a decision, but a "yes" is gated on the same contested IVIVC mapping and the magnitude at stake is small.

Strongest remaining objection:
The magnitude limb is no longer unquantified but pointed the other way by the only opened measurement of the candidate's own proposed instrument. Assi, Chrystyn, Pearson & Tarsin, Int J Pharm 2006;316(1-2):131-137 report fluticasone fine particle dose of 20.4% (SD 4.8) of labelled dose from recorded profiles of 20 severe asthmatics — CV ~24%, ±1 SD ~1.6-fold against the 10-fold ladder on which the flatness is claimed — and carried through the candidate's own convolution mechanism with Proost 2021's steepness equation this yields a max-slope ratio of ~1.02–1.08x (~1.10–1.36x for the Turbuhaler's ~56% CV). If that is the true dispersion, answer branch (ii) is reachable at a desk from two published papers, and the question's premise that there is a material gap to apportion fails. The escape — that fine particle dose omits airway deposition, so true lung-dose dispersion is strictly larger by an unmeasured amount — is plausible, is the reason both adversaries scored this Partial rather than Unresolved, and is unsourced in this run.
Promotion requires: all three of (1) the unrun Disguise queries executed with no prior found — Chrystyn's own vocabulary ("Electronic Lung", "ex vivo emitted dose at the patient's own inhalation profile") crossed with clinical outcomes, plus the Dundee thesis "Personalising inhaled corticosteroid dose response in persistent asthma", the Mouksassi PAGE abstract and Bentham 10.2174/157488507779422392 opened; (2) a per-patient ICS LUNG-DEPOSITION dispersion figure from an opened imaging or scintigraphy source in a comparable population, set against a lung-deposition comparator rather than against the device-exit fine-particle-dose spread — verification established that the "24-56%" band in the original wording is a reader's derivation from the four mean (SD) pairs of fine particle dose as % label claim in Assi/Tarsin 2006 alone, mixing two drugs and two devices, and is a different measurand from deposition, so the original comparison could not have discharged anything; the condition is therefore: open at least two imaging sources reporting a per-patient deposition CV for a conventional (non-extrafine) ICS formulation in asthma, and show that CV is materially above the deposition CV implied by STORM's 25.50% +/- 6.81% (about 26.7%, n = 9, extrafine, derived not published), so the slope-ratio bound is not already settled near 1 — if conventional-formulation deposition CV is not materially above it, attack 1 becomes a published answer, attack 4 becomes fatal and the entry goes to Rejected rather than Validated; and (3) V2 rewritten so instrument and estimand match (exposure declared as emitted dose, or an explicit deposition model carrying a severity interaction) with a pre-specified threshold for "materially steeper", which is what would restore well-posedness to the 3/3 that Validated requires.

Suggested first step toward an answer (pointer only — do not take it):
Open the scintigraphy/imaging deposition literature for ICS and extract a per-patient lung-dose CV with its stated uncertainty, then put it through Proost 2021's steepness equation alongside Assi 2006's emitted-dose CV. That single comparison decides whether the question has a gap to apportion or has already been answered at a desk, and it is cheaper than any trial-level step.

ID: UQ-20261017-37
Date: 2026-10-17
Status: Rejected
Domain(s): Medicine — pragmatic clinical-trial methodology (cluster-randomised and stepped-wedge trials in health systems). Neighbours searched: biostatistics/causal inference (bipartite experiments, partial and cross-cluster interference), multilevel statistics (multiple-membership and cross-classified random effects), psychotherapy-trial methodology (therapist effects/contamination), health-workforce research, hospital epidemiology (HCW mobility from EHR identifiers), education economics, development economics, antimicrobial stewardship, German and French.
Question (canonical): V2 (Gate 1 reformulation, the one permitted; V1 in the record) — restricted to clinician-mediated interventions and defining overlap contemporaneously (one clinician delivering care in the same calendar window in two clusters in different treatment states): (a) across a pre-declared frame of health-system cluster-randomised and stepped-wedge trials, what is the distribution of (i) the share of clusters with at least one such clinician and (ii) the share of patient-contacts they deliver, measured from trial rosters or payer/EHR provider identifiers rather than from the trial report's prose; and (b) in trials whose provider identifiers are retrievable, how far does re-analysis under a crossed clinician random effect or a bipartite-interference-aware estimator move the point estimate and interval against the published analysis?
Alternative formulations: Is the cluster the right randomisation unit when the agents who deliver the intervention practise in several clusters at once? / Measured on real trials rather than assumed away as "contamination", how large is the bias from clinicians who work on both sides of a cluster randomisation?
Motivating gap: Intake (presupposition inversion): cluster and stepped-wedge designs are justified by between-cluster independence, shared staff were believed to appear only as a listed limitation and never as a measured quantity, and statistics now has estimators for bipartite delivery. Gate 2 falsified the premise: the phenomenon is named ("therapist contamination") and counted twice in the candidate's own literature, and the bias limb has one published, explicitly indeterminate answer. Gate 4 falsified it a second time in two further vocabularies. What is left unpublished is the instrument (provider identifiers, not text), the denominators (clusters and patient-contacts, not articles), the frame (health-system pragmatic/SW-CRT, not mental-health complex interventions) and the within-trial re-analysis.
Presuppositions: 1. Clinician-to-cluster affiliation during the trial is recoverable from rosters/administrative data — CONTESTED at Gate 2 (only 57% of 100 protocols name who delivered the intervention, so unrecoverable for a literature-assembled frame), then EVIDENCED at Gate 4 for the within-trial route (Wilson-Aggarwal et al. 2022 locate staff by ward and day from Epic pseudonymous HCW identifiers plus door-access logs). 2. Exposure travels with the clinician — CONTESTED; V2 repairs it by restricting to clinician-mediated interventions, but V2's contemporaneity rule then excludes the larger channel for durable training exposure (trained in period 1, practising in a control cluster in period 3), so the instrument undercounts what it prices. 3. Published estimates assume no cross-cluster agent sharing — ESTABLISHED. 4. Some trials permit a crossed or interference-aware re-analysis — the crossed random effect is estimable; the causal interference contrast is NOT identified from a single realised cluster-level assignment, which the record concedes. 5. Overlap biases rather than only inflating variance — CONTESTED, with a published prior pointing the other way. 6. V1's "or period" limb is ~100% by design in a stepped-wedge trial and is the already-named quantity carry-over; V2 drops it.
What would count as an answer: A measured overlap distribution (clusters with any contemporaneous cross-state clinician; share of patient-contacts they deliver) over a pre-declared frame, from provider identifiers, plus at least one re-analysis under a crossed-clinician or interference-aware model reporting the movement of the estimate and interval. Overlap near zero retires the listed limitation for that frame; overlap common with no movement answers the bias limb in the negative. Both directions informative; the frame-level limb is executable only by trialists or a consortium holding site-level provider data, which is what caps well-posedness.
Novelty — queries run (query → one-line result): 29 documented queries (11 at Gate 2, 9 per adversary, every adversary query in a vocabulary Gate 2 did not use) and 13 pages opened on publisher/repository routes with no PMC or Europe PMC attempt; full lists in batches/2026-10-17-1619/UQ-20261017-37-record.md and the two adversary logs. Most informative: "contamination in cluster randomised trials clinicians treating patients in both arms measured" → the on-point own-field prior (Magill et al. 2019) plus the Jacobsen & Wood contamination-risk framework; "proportion of physicians practicing at multiple hospitals multi-site practice measured fraction" → the workforce multisite fraction is already published (Xierali 2018, 63.2%, mean 3.3 sites); "cross-classified random effects cluster randomized trial providers not nested within clusters" (adversary 2, a vocabulary Gate 2 never tried) → the kill hit, Moerbeek & Safarkhani 2018 JEBS, which formalises professionals crossed with randomised clusters and states the candidate's limb-(a) parameter "are hardly available in the literature"; German/French contamination queries (both adversaries) → only the same P1 and Torgerson BMJ 2001, no non-English-only literature; "healthcare worker movement between hospital wards ... provider identifiers" → a mature measured-HCW-mobility literature from the candidate's own instrument; "proportion of control cluster patients treated by clinician who also worked in intervention cluster trial administrative data overlap" and the contact-weighted answer-shaped query → no hit, the measured quantity itself appears nowhere.
Novelty — nearest prior formulations (3, with sources): P1. Magill et al., "A scoping review of the problems and solutions associated with contamination in trials of complex interventions in mental health", BMC Med Res Methodol 19:4 (2019), doi 10.1186/s12874-018-0646-z — unit: the trial article (234; 93 cluster-allocated); endpoint: author-described contamination process plus participant-level control-arm receipt; comparator: within-study cluster-vs-participant allocation (4 trials, 21 outcomes); estimand: descriptive counts, median contamination, informal effect-magnitude comparison. Numbers verified verbatim twice on the publisher route: "staff delivering the active intervention in the control arm (n = 82, 35%)", 76 of those 82 citing one clinician delivering both treatments (unit corrected at verification from the record's "76/234"), median contamination 13% (IQR 5–33%) in 23 trials, the both-level trials "did not find any evidence for differences in effect size estimates", "a systematic review of this particular trial design is needed". P2. Moerbeek & Safarkhani, "The Design of Cluster Randomized Trials With Random Cross-Classifications", J Educ Behav Stat 43(2):159–181 (2018) — unit: the design (sample-size/power); endpoint: required N and optimal allocation when "a second random factor, such as the professionals delivering the intervention, is crossed with the randomized clusters", with a "complete" design in which "each professional delivers both conditions" and a "partial" design that "is less efficient"; comparator: competing designs; estimand: design efficiency given assumed variance components, with crossed-professional ICC "hardly available in the literature" and assumed "without further justification"; it re-analyses no outcome data and reports no measured proportion. P3. Keogh-Brown et al., "Contamination in trials of educational interventions", Health Technol Assess 11(43) (2007), doi 10.3310/hta11430 — unit: the trial, across prior systematic reviews; endpoint: effect of contamination on magnitude and precision, and its mechanisms; comparator: trials that did vs did not avoid contamination; estimand: whether avoidance yields larger effects. Abstract read verbatim: "Few relevant studies quantified contamination", CRTs "might produce biases greater than or similar to those of individually randomised trials", CACE is "an appropriate way to adjust for contamination if it can be measured", "it is a priority to report the extent, nature and effects of contamination" (report body not read; no claim that it measured clinician cross-cluster overlap). Also real and verified but adjacent rather than prior: Jacobsen & Wood 2020 (protocol-level, 14/100 high risk, 10 therapist-related, 57% ascertainment ceiling; not re-opened by either adversary), Xierali 2018 (workforce multisite, no trial/arm/randomisation), Wilson-Aggarwal et al., Commun Med 2:165 (2022) (instrument exists, no trial or arms), Torgerson BMJ 2001 (participant contamination only, "does not discuss contamination arising from people who deliver the intervention"), Walwyn et al. arXiv:2601.16318, Leung arXiv:2310.18836, Brennan et al. arXiv:2210.16415, Chattopadhyay et al. arXiv:2312.03268 (no health-provider application), Jenney & Lohr AoAS 2009 (teachers nested, agents not shared).
Novelty — how this differs from each: vs P1 — P1 counts ARTICLES whose text describes a clinician delivering both treatments in a mental-health frame; the candidate counts CLUSTERS and PATIENT-CONTACTS from provider identifiers in a health-system frame, and re-analyses one trial's own data instead of comparing magnitudes across allocation levels. An instrument, denominator and frame swap on the same object; P1's own bias limb is the candidate's limb (b), asked and left open. vs P2 — P2 is design/power with assumed variance components and no measurement; the candidate would measure the parameter P2 says is unavailable. That is the candidate's limb (a) being explicitly requested in print, in a second field, which makes it asked-and-open rather than un-asked. vs P3 — P3 asked the bias question nineteen years earlier for educational (i.e. clinician-training) interventions, compared contaminated and uncontaminated trials, and asked trialists to report contamination's extent; the candidate differs only in instrument and in offering a crossed-random-effect refit where P3 prescribed CACE.
Novelty confidence: Low
Significance — consequence: If overlap is common and re-analysis moves estimates, the cluster is the wrong randomisation unit for clinician-mediated interventions, CONSORT's cluster extension and SW-CRT reporting need a provider-affiliation item, and a crossed-clinician sensitivity model becomes an expected SAP row. If overlap is common and nothing moves (the direction P1's weaker test already points), a routinely listed limitation is retired with a number. If overlap is near zero, the same, more cheaply. Independent of the bias limb, the measured crossing fraction and professional-level ICC would supply the power-calculation input P2 states is missing.
Significance — audience: Cluster and stepped-wedge methodologists, the NIH Pragmatic Trials Collaboratory and comparable embedded-trial programmes, CONSORT/SPIRIT cluster-extension authors, CTU trial statisticians, and the design-methods authors of P2 who cannot parameterise their own power calculations. Institutionally evidenced: NIHR commissioned a full HTA report on this concern in 2007 that ended by calling measurement a priority.
Significance — fecundity: What estimand is defined when the delivery agent, not the unit, carries exposure (the bipartite analogue of the informative-cluster-size debate); should clinician-intervention combinations be randomised instead of clusters; does provider overlap explain part of the attenuation of pragmatic-trial effects; what is the design-efficiency cost of restricting a trial to non-overlapping clinicians (P2 gives the direction, not the price).
Significance — anchoring: P1's unresolved bias limb and P3's 2007 call; carry-over and time-varying effects in stepped-wedge designs; identifiability of interference from a single cluster-level assignment; informative cluster size and the CRT estimand debate; measured HCW mobility in hospital epidemiology.
Reason for silence: Offered mechanism — measurement-access gap crossed with a disciplinary boundary, plus a trialist incentive not to quantify a limitation that can only weaken an estimate. It does not survive: it explains why the measurement is unexecuted, not why the question went unasked, and the question is demonstrably not unasked (twice in medicine, once in educational statistics). The instrument-scarcity limb also fails, since hospital epidemiologists already derive staff-by-ward-by-day from the same EHR provider identifiers trial teams hold. Only the incentive limb stands, and it accounts for a missing answer rather than a missing question.

Both load-bearing sentences are verbatim: "Few relevant studies quantified contamination" (abstract Results, p iii) and "When conducting such trials in future, it is a priority to report the extent, nature and effects of contamination" (Conclusions, p iii, repeated p xi); CACE is "an appropriate way to adjust for contamination if it can be measured". P3 therefore does pose the candidate's bias limb and does ask for its measurement. Two corrections, both narrowing what P3 ESTABLISHED rather than what it ASKED: (i) the direction is MIXED, not one-way — Chapter 2's all-studies L'Abbe analysis gives medians 4.384 (contamination avoided) against 7.354 (not avoided) and concludes that trials avoiding contamination "tended to have larger effects", while the same chapter concludes "there is no clear evidence that the effectiveness estimate in trials that do not avoid contamination is biased", and the high-quality reminder subset runs the other way (Table 5 medians 11.6 cluster against 3.783 individual, on 5 and 6 trials); the oral-health trial's plaque-surface contrast (-16.7%, 95% CI -25.7 to -7.7 cluster, against -4.5%, 95% CI -12.7 to 3.7 individual) is allowed by the report itself to "could have been due to biased measurement rather than contamination"; (ii) P3 never counts cross-arm delivery either (NOT FOUND across what was read) — its 84 dentists are a count of dentists, and "the same doctor administering different arms of the trial" appears only as a criterion for classing a trial as likely contaminated, with no tally. So P3 asks the question and leaves limb (a) unmeasured, which is what routing turns on.
V2. Magill (P1) CONFIRMED on every figure checked, with one unit correction: 234 studies, 93 (39.7%) cluster-allocated, n=82 (35%) with staff delivering the active intervention in the control arm, and n=76 — which is 76 OF THOSE 82, not of the 234 — citing one clinician delivering both treatments. The entry's and the kill's "76/234" was wrong and is corrected here and in the routing row. The median contamination of 13% (IQR 5-33%) is over 23 binary-outcome trials and its unit is CONTROL-ARM PARTICIPANTS, not clusters or clinicians (27 trials attempted to quantify contamination, 4 of them on continuous outcomes). The null bias finding rests on 4 trials and 21 outcomes, attenuated under participant-level allocation in 8 of 21 with one tie and "just under half" in the anticipated direction — a thinner basis than "did not find any evidence for differences in effect size estimates" reads as. "a systematic review of this particular trial design is needed" is verbatim.
V3. Moerbeek & Safarkhani (P2) REFUTED AS THE KILL USED IT, confirmed as the record used it (JEBS 2018;43(2):159-181, doi 10.3102/1076998617730303 — the entry's DOI stands; a first-guess 10.3102/1076998617741090 is wrong; read as the SAGE full-text PDF on two independent fetches that agreed). The crossing is in the paper verbatim ("As not all soldiers from the same unit are treated by the same professional, units and professionals are crossed with each other"), and so is the scarcity sentence — but it is about VARIANCE COMPONENTS, not overlap: "For cluster randomized trials with crossed random effects, such estimates are hardly available in the literature, but at least one can use estimates from cluster randomized trials without a random cross-classification". The paper issues NO call to measure how often clinicians cross clusters (NOT FOUND; its only future-work ask is simulation of imperfect hierarchies and the supply of prior ICC estimates), and reports no measured crossing fraction and no professional-level ICC of its own (NOT FOUND; the worked example assumes ru=.3 from Mulligan's published power analysis and rv=.1, rw=.05 "without further justification"). P2 is therefore a demand for the professional-level ICC — the second of the two parameters this entry's consequence paragraph names — and NOT a third asking of limb (a). That claim is struck from attack 2 and from the strongest-objection paragraph.
V4. Effect on the verdict: NONE. Attack 2 is Unresolved on Keogh-Brown and Magill alone, both now verified at first hand in the sources themselves: the candidate's object is asked twice in its own literature, once with a call for a systematic review and once with a call to report contamination's extent, and neither answers it. Rejected stands, on a narrower ground than the batch wrote.
V5. Routing unchanged but amended before appending, and the two adjacent sources behind the row were re-opened: Jacobsen & Wood 2020 (J Clin Epidemiol 124:8-15, doi 10.1016/j.jclinepi.2020.04.005, UCL author PDF) is 14 of 100 protocols at high contamination risk with 10 OF THOSE 14 therapist-related (71%), not 10 of 100, and 57 of 100 protocols state clearly who delivered the intervention (13 no, 30 unclear); Xierali 2018 (JABFM 31(2):260-269, doi 10.3122/jabfm.2018.02.170287) is 63.2% multi-site with a mean of 3.3 sites over 20,116 Georgia Medicaid-registered physicians (6,116 excluded) — a marginal workforce rate, not a trial cohort — and it carries an internal inconsistency, its Discussion stating that two thirds of Georgia physicians practised in one service location against the 63.2% multi-site headline. Both stay recorded as adjacent, not prior. The row names the professional-level ICC, which is P2's actual demand, rather than a crossing fraction P2 never asks for.
Scores: Well-posedness 2/3 · Significance 2/3 (adversary 2 argues for 3/3 on sourced demand from P2; left at 2/3 because it does not bear on the verdict)
Strongest remaining objection: Disguise, Unresolved independently by both adversaries and the ground the verdict rests on. The candidate's object — do clinicians who straddle the arms of a cluster trial of a clinician-delivered intervention contaminate it, and does that move the effect estimate — has been posed in print at least three times: Keogh-Brown et al. (HTA 11(43), 2007) set out to quantify the effect on magnitude and precision, compared trials that did and did not avoid contamination, found "Few relevant studies quantified contamination" and called reporting its extent "a priority"; Magill et al. (2019) re-asked both limbs, counted 76 of the 82 articles describing one clinician delivering both treatments and called for a systematic review; and Moerbeek & Safarkhani (2018), in a vocabulary Gate 2 never searched, formalise professionals crossed with randomised clusters and ask in print for the professional-level ICC, stating such estimates "are hardly available in the literature" (verification struck the kill's further claim that this paper requests limb (a): it asks for variance components, issues no call to measure crossing frequency, and so supports the entry's significance case rather than its Disguise kill — the kill therefore rests on Keogh-Brown and Magill, both verified at first hand). What the candidate adds is a better instrument (provider identifiers), better denominators (clusters and patient-contacts) and a narrower frame — a covariate/instrument swap on an asked question, which this ledger rejects even when the exact variant is unmeasured. Secondary and non-fatal: attack 7 is also Unresolved by both, and the causal half of limb (b) is not identified from a single realised cluster-level assignment, leaving a model-sensitivity contrast where the significance case promises a bias estimate. Caveats on the kill, recorded rather than hidden: P3 was read at abstract level only during the batch, and at executive-summary plus Chapters 1-2 level at verification, which confirmed both of its load-bearing sentences, Leroux & Beretvas 2012 at title level only, and P2 (Jacobsen & Wood) and P3 (Xierali) of the record were not independently re-opened — none of those absences is counted as a check that passed, and none is load-bearing, since the two fatal readings rest on pages that were opened in full (Magill on the publisher route, twice; Moerbeek & Safarkhani as the SAGE PDF).
Suggested first step toward an answer (pointer only — do not take it): not for this ledger. The routed limb's first step is the systematic review P1 explicitly calls for, which is executable from the public record; the measurement limb's is a single embedded trial that already holds provider identifiers reporting its own cluster-level and contact-weighted overlap as one worked case.
Routing (if rejected as already-asked): YES, one row to ledger/routed-open-problems.md, for the asked-and-open limb only — whether realised cross-arm clinician exposure moves cluster-trial effect estimates, together with the empirical crossing fraction and professional-level ICC that Moerbeek & Safarkhani 2018 state is unavailable. Limb (a) at article and protocol level is asked and partially answered (P1, Jacobsen & Wood) and is NOT routed; the disguised-known framing itself is not routed.

ID: UQ-20261017-38
Date: 2026-10-17
Status: Rejected
Domain(s): Medicine — clinical prediction models / clinical decision support; method from software engineering (differential / N-version testing of independent implementations of one specification). Owning literatures are mHealth safety, medical-app assessment and clinical pharmacology, not clinical epidemiology.
Question (canonical): For a pre-declared set of published clinical risk scores each carrying a published action threshold, do independently written implementations return the same value for the same patient, at what rate do they disagree enough to cross the threshold, and what share of those crossings is implementation error rather than under-specification in the source publication? (V1, the one permitted Gate 1 reformulation, adds a pre-run partition of the input space into spec-determined and spec-undetermined regions, a pre-declared input-sampling rule weighted to boundary/unit/missing cases, and a chance-corrected adjudication statistic; V0 retained in the record, which is circular in using "faithful implementation" on inputs the publication does not determine.)
Alternative formulations:
1. Is a published clinical risk score a well-defined function of its inputs, or only a sketch each implementer completes differently?
2. How often does which calculator you open, rather than which patient you have, decide which side of the threshold the patient lands on?
3. (Method-field wording) What does N-version differential testing of deployed score implementations against their published specification find, and how much divergence is specification under-determination rather than defect?
Motivating gap: Intake held that software engineering routinely asks whether independent implementations of one specification agree while medicine treats each score as a fixed function and only compares *different* models (Framingham vs QRISK vs PCE). Gate 2 overturned the gap: the question is asked and substantially answered in medicine's own journals and in the method-owning field, in registers the intake did not try ("calculator app accuracy", "systematic assessment", "partition violation", "online GFR calculator accuracy"). Neamtiu 2023 states the intake's gap in its own abstract and then closes it.
Presuppositions:
1. Divergence from the published description is a defect, not local design choice — established in practice; contested for localised EHR builds, and additionally version-indexed (CKD-EPI 2009 vs 2021; FRAX v3.8 vs v4), a confound the record never named. Adversary 1 Partial; adversary 2 holds V1's pre-declared publication per score defuses it.
2. >= 3 inspectable independent implementations exist per score — over-established: 47 CKD-EPI calculators, 90 Android apps over 12 scores, 46 insulin-dose apps, 23 opioid-conversion apps. Fails only for proprietary EHR builds, which V1 excludes from S.
3. Disagreements can be adjudicated into coding error vs under-specification — established and already done: P1 separates specification from implementation error sources; N1 adjudicates all 28 errors to cause. CORRECTION (adversary 2, verified in P1 §4.3/§5.4.1): P1 *does* report multiple-rater agreement (100% across three analysts), so the record's "no inter-rater statistic is reported" is wrong and the candidate's increment shrinks to a chance-corrected statistic on the error-source categories specifically.
4. Each score has an action threshold whose crossing changes an action — true by construction of S; the record's supporting citation overreaches (P1's "Meets or Exceeds Threshold" column is undefined in the paper) but the question does not depend on it.
5. A defensible input grid including awkward regions exists — established, and the awkward regions are exactly where every prior already found the defects (SOFA Bilirubin=12.0, Creatinine=5.0; APACHE II Age=44; HEART Age=65; CKD-EPI ethnicity switch and both creatinine units), which weakens the claim that grid design is open.
What would count as an answer: measured pairwise and set-wise any-difference rate and threshold-crossing rate across >= 3 implementations per score on a pre-declared sample, reported separately over the two regions, plus the adjudicated error/under-specification split with an agreement statistic, plus a per-score under-specification audit. Near-zero crossings on a grid that genuinely includes the awkward regions answers it in the negative — and that branch is already partly in hand (P2: 98.6% output accuracy, Child-Pugh errors did not change class; N2: limits of agreement <1% between two FRAX implementations on 1,254 patients).
Novelty — queries run (query → one-line result): 29 distinct queries — 11 at Gate 2, 9 by adversary 1, 9 by adversary 2, all Disguise queries new to the record. Full lists: batches/2026-10-17-1619/UQ-20261017-38-record.md and UQ-20261017-38-adversary-1.md / -adversary-2.md. Most informative: (a) "accuracy of medical calculator apps errors incorrect results validation smartphone clinical scores" → P1 and P2 immediately, both opened — THE decisive Gate 2 query; (b) "agreement between independent implementations of the same clinical risk score discordance reclassification threshold" (the mandated own-field obvious-title query, in the candidate's own words) → nothing on point, the instructive miss: "independent implementations" is not medicine's vocabulary; (c) "eGFR online calculators discrepancies same creatinine different results websites apps comparison" (adversary 1) and "eGFR calculator discrepancies ... same creatinine value different reported result laboratory" (adversary 2) → independently surfaced N1 (Seiberth 2020), opened at the publisher on the first call by both; (d) "FRAX smartphone apps compared with official FRAX web tool agreement discordance" → N2 (Yang 2023), the pairwise estimand executed on real patients; (e) "N-version programming / software diversity ... medical device clinical algorithm" (both adversaries, the method field's own term of art) → no medical hit, so the transplant was made without the method's name and the name adds nothing; (f) "risk score built into electronic health record does not match published algorithm vendor implementation audit" → no build-fidelity audit found, the candidate's one uncovered slice; (g) "proportion of published prediction models reported with enough detail to make individual risk predictions" (the mandated fraction query) → the TRIPOD/Collins reporting-adequacy corpus, COULD NOT READ (fetch budget), so no published fraction is recorded here in either direction. Access: 13 fetches across three agents; doi.org/10.1145/3610912 and both Springer routes to Haffey 2013 returned CLIENT_ERROR; no PMC or Europe PMC route attempted anywhere.
Novelty — nearest prior formulations (3, with sources):
P1. Rahaman S, Samuel R, Neamtiu I, "Diagnosing Medical Score Calculator Apps", Proc. ACM IMWUT 7(3) Art. 118, 2023, DOI 10.1145/3610912 — OPENED IN FULL (web.njit.edu/~ineamtiu/pubs/ubicomp23rahaman.pdf), and re-opened and spot-checked by adversary 2. Unit: (app, score, input configuration) over 90 Android apps and 12 scores, plus (score, published reference table). Endpoint: partition violations in the published specification and in app GUIs, and incorrect computed scores. Comparator: the published reference table after the authors repair its own defects — a specification oracle, explicitly not other implementations. Estimand: defect counts, no declared input distribution (8 coverage + 3 non-overlap violations in 5 of 12 published tables; 23 coverage, 32 non-overlap, 16 calculation errors in apps; 6 apps fixed after disclosure). Separates specification from implementation error, names irreducible ambiguity in a source paper, discusses threshold straddling, reports 100% multiple-rater agreement (not chance-corrected), gives no quantitative threshold-crossing rate, and does not name EHR builds as a limitation.
P2. Bierbrier R, Lo V, Wu RC, "Evaluation of the Accuracy of Smartphone Medical Calculation Apps", J Med Internet Res 2014;16(2):e32 — OPENED (jmir.org/2014/2/e32). Unit: (app, function, test case), 14 apps x 13 functions x 10 shared cases = 1240 outputs, so >= 3 independent implementations of one score on one input set. Endpoint: binary match to reference. Comparator: investigators' manual Excel computation from the published definition. Estimand: accuracy proportion 98.6% (17 errors), about half clinically significant, Child-Pugh errors at low ranges and not changing class. No CIs, no inter-app agreement statistic, no threshold-crossing rate, no under-specification audit.
N1 (found by both adversaries, and the strongest killing point). Unit: (online calculator, reference case) for ONE published equation; 49 identified, 47 evaluated — I = 47. Input sample declared in advance: five hypothetical cases — two Caucasian males either side of creatinine 0.9 mg/dl, two Caucasian females either side of 0.7, one African-American male — with the 88.4 unit conversion assessed per calculator, so it reaches the ethnicity switch, both creatinine units and the branch cut-off but NOT extremes of age or missing values (ages sit in an unseen Supplementary Table S1), which is narrower than the candidate's grid; corrected at verification from the record's "the awkward regions the candidate claims as its own". Oracle: two authors independently entering the published equation into separate spreadsheets and cross-checking — the candidate's own N-version construction. Estimand: "Only 36 of 47 calculators (76.6%) produced accurate eGFR results for all reference cases"; "Eight of 47 (17.0%) calculators were considered as faulty"; "28 errors were found (range 59 to 147% of the correct eGFR value)", each adjudicated to cause (ethnicity handling, eGFR and creatinine unit conversion, BSA de-indexing, wrong equation branch below the 0.9 mg/dl cut-off, unexplained), with rounding set aside — but verification established that this taxonomy does NOT separate a calculator's coding mistake from a choice the equation leaves open, which the record wrongly read into it. Names the equation's own under-determined choices (Mosteller vs Du Bois BSA, variant selection, "There appears to be no general recommendation on an upper age limit", assay method) — but in Methods and Discussion rather than as an audit, with no sensitivity analysis of any of them, so "a per-score under-specification audit" is withdrawn at verification; the choices are named, not audited. Reports no threshold-crossing rate and no agreement statistic. (Adversary 1's own arithmetic, flagged as such: 11/47 = 23.4% wrong on at least one case, the complement of the source's figure; the source gives no uncertainty for these proportions.)
Superseded prior, kept for the record: P3 Haffey F, Brady RR, Maxwell S, "A Comparison of the Reliability of Smartphone Apps for Opioid Conversion", Drug Saf 2013;36(2):111-117 — COULD NOT READ by all three agents (doi.org and link.springer.com, both forms, CLIENT_ERROR; PMC not attempted). Grades nothing. Also found and not opened, grading nothing: N2 Yang L et al., Arch Osteoporos 2023;18:43 (opened by adversary 1: two FRAX implementations, 1,254 real patients, "excellent agreement", limits of agreement <1%, no reclassification reported); Huckvale 2015 BMC Medicine (46 insulin-dose apps); Akbar 2020 JAMIA (74 app studies, none on score calculators — the field's own statement of the silence immediately before P1 closed it); the TRIPOD/Collins reporting-adequacy corpus; eCQM vendor-implementation-variation literature; Lippi & Sanchis-Gomar, J Med Syst 2018;42(4).
Novelty — how this differs from each: vs P1 — P1 performs the under-specification audit the intake named as the candidate's most distinctive limb, for 12 scores, finds 5 of 12 published tables ill-posed with defects in exactly the boundary cells the candidate says a grid must include, separates specification from implementation defect, and discusses threshold straddling; it does not use other implementations as comparator, report rates over a declared distribution, or give a chance-corrected statistic. vs P2 — P2 executes limb (i)'s design (>= 3 implementations, one score, one shared input set) with the estimand as accuracy against an oracle rather than pairwise agreement, and limb (ii) qualitatively. vs N1 — N1 is closer to V1 than either graded prior: 47 implementations of one published equation, a pre-declared awkward-region input set, an N-version-built oracle, per-error cause adjudication and an explicit under-determination audit; it lacks only the threshold-crossing rate and the agreement statistic. vs the different-models family the intake anticipated — unchanged, not prior art; the intake was right about that family and wrong that no other family exists. After four priors opened across four registers the surviving increment is: report limb (ii) as a rate, and put a chance-corrected statistic on limb (iii).
Novelty confidence: Low
Significance — consequence: If implementation-induced threshold crossing is non-trivial, every deployment needs verification before use and journals must publish executable specifications; if near-zero outside the spec-undetermined region, the concern retires. Discounted heavily: the answer is substantially in hand and points one way — implementations are mostly right, a minority grossly wrong for nameable reasons (units, ethnicity branch, BSA de-indexing, boundary cells), and published specifications are ill-posed at boundaries in a substantial minority of scores.
Significance — audience: Real and demonstrably responsive — P1's disclosure led to 6 app fixes; N1 concludes calculators "need more thorough evaluation after deployment"; MDCalc fields inter-implementation divergence in its own FAQ; score authors and TRIPOD, EHR vendors and clinical-content teams, regulators under CDS software policy. But the audience has been told this five times over a decade, and no prior shows anyone would act differently on the candidate's specific increment.
Significance — fecundity: Whether scores should ship as executable reference implementations with conformance suites; whether a score's under-determined region predicts inter-site outcome heterogeneity; whether EHR localisation is defect or legitimate adaptation; the cost of a certification regime. These remain askable; the EHR-build limb has the only real head-room.
Significance — anchoring: mHealth app-safety corpus (P1, P2, P3, Huckvale, Akbar); clinical-pharmacology calculator-accuracy work (N1); TRIPOD/Collins reporting adequacy (unread here); eCQM vendor-implementation variation (unopened); N-version / differential testing as a method family, which both adversaries confirmed has never been pointed at clinical scores under its own name.
Reason for silence: The premise fails — there is no silence to explain. The question was asked under at least four names (Drug Safety 2013, JMIR 2014, Eur J Clin Pharmacol 2020, ACM IMWUT 2023), in four registers that do not cite each other. What needs explaining is the intake's search failure, and that mechanism is diagnostic for this ledger: a vocabulary boundary *inside* the target field. The mandated own-field obvious-title query phrased in the candidate's own words missed the prior art; the same query in the register the field actually prints found it immediately. A search failure is not a silence, so Gate 4's rule to treat the novelty finding as suspect and return to Gate 2 applies — which is where this entry already sits.

V3. Seiberth (N1) — the RECORD was right and the first verification reader was wrong on the under-determination limb; two of the kill's four claimed attributes nonetheless fall. Settled on a full-text re-read at the publisher (2 fetches). I = 47 counts ONLINE CALCULATORS (49 found, 2 returned nothing) across 11 countries, for the 2009 creatinine CKD-EPI equation, against FIVE hypothetical reference cases — two Caucasian males either side of creatinine 0.9 mg/dl, two Caucasian females either side of 0.7, one African-American male — with the 88.4 unit conversion assessed per calculator. The oracle is as the record described: the equation entered into two separate Excel sheets independently by two authors (SS, DC) and compared, with no stated rule for resolving disagreement. Results confirmed: 36 of 47 (76.6%) accurate on all cases; 11 not, of which 3 were excluded (2 imposing a 70-year age limit, 1 declining African-American ethnicity while saying so), leaving 8 (17.0%) faulty with 28 errors spanning 59 to 147% of the correct value. WHAT FALLS: (i) the paper does NOT distinguish a calculator's own coding mistake from a choice the published equation leaves open — NOT FOUND on a full read; what it has is a defect taxonomy (ethnicity handling 4; indexed/non-indexed conversion applied in the wrong direction 2, carrying 10 errors; creatinine unit conversion 1, 5 errors; wrong unit label 1, 5 errors; wrong equation branch below the creatinine cut-off 1; unexplained 2); and (ii) there is no under-determination AUDIT and no sensitivity analysis of the open choices. WHAT HOLDS, against the first reader's NOT FOUND: the paper does name the implementer-undetermined choices, in Methods and Discussion rather than as an audit — BSA by "Mosteller's or Du Bois'" equation, matched to whichever the calculator used, with only 5 of 47 computing BSA from height and weight; the variant question (several equations by sex, ethnicity and creatinine, or one); the verbatim "there appears to be no general recommendation on an upper age limit"; and the creatinine assay, with 9 of 47 explicitly requesting standardised creatinine and the Discussion contrasting enzymatic against Jaffe. (iii) No stage-reclassification or threshold rate (NOT FOUND); the cutoffs are error magnitude (>= 1 ml/min/1.73 m2, sensitivity at 2, 5 and 10), with CKD misstaging raised anecdotally and one worked metformin example (a true 42.7 reported as 51.6 instead of 35.2). Also new: N1's input set is NARROWER than the kill implied — five cases, ages only in an unseen Supplementary Table S1, no extremes or missing values in the main text — and "11 not accurate" and "8 faulty" are different numbers, the three excluded on exactly the grounds the candidate would class as specification latitude.
V4. A FOURTH prior, closer than any graded one on the limb this entry reserved for the candidate: Hwang S, Thomas S, Williams H, Bar-Or A, Sharma V, Buijs F, Perrone C, Mowery DL, "Same Inputs, Different EDSS: Measuring Specification Drift in Clinical Scoring Pipelines", medRxiv preprint posted 2026-07-07, doi 10.64898/2026.06.25.26356350 — surfaced at title level by the implementations survey and opened here. Three EDSS calculators (a prompt-executed natural-language specification, an LLM-generated Python specification, and an open-source canonical port of a published JavaScript version) run on the same extracted functional-system subscores over 57,604 progress notes from 5,231 patients at one site. Exact agreement 98.1% between the executable specification and the canonical port (99.8% within 0.5 EDSS) against 82.8 to 84.2% for the natural-language specification; Wasserstein distance 0.014 against 0.170 to 0.183; on repeat testing 15.8% of notes (n = 9,106) gave a median natural-language value differing from the executable one. It HAS the boundary-flip analysis, which is the candidate's limb (ii) as a rate — Table 3 is "proportion of notes whose category membership changes between calculators" — though Table 3's cells were unreadable here and Appendix B bounds reclassification at EDSS 4.0 and 5.5-6.0 as "rare (<= 0.85%)". It does NOT give a formal under-specification-versus-defect split, separating systematic from stochastic disagreement instead (42.5% systematic over 120 vectors, 27.5% within-prompt variable), and it reports a chance-corrected statistic only against annotators (quadratic weighted kappa about 0.98 for each calculator), none between calculators; its canonical reference is said to encode specific interpretation choices, so it is a reference and not a gold standard. Its own cited nearest priors are computable-phenotype portability (Mo 2015, Kirby 2016, Rasmussen 2014, Pacheco 2023) and differential and property-based testing (McKeeman 1998; Claessen & Hughes 2000; MacIver 2019) — the method family both adversaries reported had never been pointed at clinical scores under its own name, now pointed at them by name three months before this batch. The one respect in which it is not the candidate: its three implementations are two LLM-derived artefacts and one port, not independently human-written software.
V5. Net effect on the verdict: NONE, and the surviving increment is smaller than the entry claimed. Of the two statistics named as unreported anywhere — a threshold-crossing rate as a rate, and a chance-corrected statistic on the adjudication — the first is now executed for one score by the EDSS preprint and partially tabulated (without a stated rate) by P1, leaving only the second unoccupied. Rejected stands.
Scores: Well-posedness 3/3 · Significance 2/3
Strongest remaining objection: Disguise, Unresolved by both adversaries and verified at first hand after the batch. The candidate's object is asked and substantially executed in at least four registers that do not cite each other. Rahaman et al. (ACM IMWUT 7(3) Art. 118, 2023) audits the published specifications themselves across 12 scores, finds 5 of them ill-posed in exactly the boundary cells the candidate says a grid must include, separates a defect in the source publication from a defect in the app in so many words, discusses threshold straddling and carries a threshold column over its 16 calculation errors. Bierbrier et al. (JMIR 2014;16(2):e32) executes limb (i)'s design — 14 independent implementations, 13 scores, one shared input set, 1,240 outputs — against an investigator-computed oracle. Hwang et al. (medRxiv, 2026-07-07, doi 10.64898/2026.06.25.26356350) runs three calculators of one published scale over 57,604 notes from 5,231 patients and reports the boundary-flip analysis as a table, which is limb (ii) as a rate, naming differential and property-based testing as its method ancestry. And Seiberth et al. 2020 (Eur J Clin Pharmacol 76(10):1465-1470, opened at the publisher by both adversaries on the first call and re-read in full at verification) matches the candidate on three attributes rather than the four the batch claimed: I = 47 independent implementations of one published equation, an oracle built by two authors independently implementing it and cross-checking, and per-error cause adjudication — but on a five-case input set with no extremes or missing values, with NO separation of coding defect from specification latitude, NO under-determination audit (it names the open choices in Methods and Discussion, including the verbatim "there appears to be no general recommendation on an upper age limit", without auditing them), and no threshold-crossing rate. What the candidate adds across the four is one statistic nobody has reported: a chance-corrected agreement figure on the error-source adjudication. That is a reporting increment on an asked and largely answered question, not an un-asked question.
Suggested first step toward an answer (pointer only — do not take it): Not applicable; the question is rejected. For the one slice with head-room — EHR vendor build fidelity — the pointer is to read the eGFR EHR-recomputation study adversary 2 surfaced by title (indexed PMC6311049, "Comparison of automated and retrospectively calculated estimated glomerular filtration rate in electronic health record data") by a non-PMC route before treating that slice as untouched.
Routing (if rejected as already-asked): Nothing routes. The EHR-build-fidelity slice is not the candidate and is not routed from here: adversary 2 struck its stated provenance (P1's limitations do not name it) and found a title-level candidate prior that may already occupy it, unread because PMC is hard-blocked and no publisher route was identified. ID: UQ-20261017-39
Date: 2026-10-17
Status: Rejected
Domain(s): Medicine — ward care of the deteriorating patient, clinical monitoring and early-warning scores. Method-owning neighbours: clinical prediction-model methodology (calibration/transportability) and biostatistics of informative observation processes.
Question (canonical): In a ward cohort carrying, on the same patients and hours, both continuous device-derived vital signs and concurrent routine clinician-scheduled observation sets, with outcomes ascertained independently of both streams: under a pre-declared aggregation rule (primary worst-value per 1-hour window; sensitivity median / time-above-threshold and 5/15/60/240-min windows) and restricted to the parameters common to both streams, what are the realised calibration-in-the-large, calibration slope, discrimination, alert rate per patient-day, PPV and lead time of unchanged published NEWS2 thresholds on each stream; what recalibration restores the intermittent stream's operating point on the continuous stream; and — tested within the intermittent stream alone — does observation intensity carry prognostic information beyond the recorded values, i.e. how much of the score's apparent prognostic value is carried by the timing of the observations rather than the physiology they recorded? (V1; reformulated once at Gate 1, V0 in the record.)
Alternative formulations:
- Is an early-warning score a measurement of the patient, or partly a measurement of how often somebody decided to measure the patient?
- Under continuous ward monitoring, what are the realised alert rate, PPV and lead time of unchanged early-warning thresholds, and what recalibration restores the published operating point?
Motivating gap: Ward observation frequency is clinician-chosen and rises with concern, so every ward EWS was fitted to values recorded at moments selected partly by prognosis; continuous wearables remove that selection while hospitals feed the new stream into the same scores. Anchoring anomaly (postoperative-hypoxaemia continuous-monitoring literature, Sun et al. 2015) recalled only, never opened — unverified.
Presuppositions: P1 observation times informative given values — ESTABLISHED (Jarvis 2015; Agniel 2018). P2 device and nurse measure a substitutable measurand — FALSE at the magnitude that matters (van Rossum device−nurse RR +9.4 breaths/min, ~2–3 NEWS2 points; Wilson RR within ±3/min in 38.5% of pairs; Imperial n=500 RR ICC 0.20; no consciousness or air/oxygen item on Wilson's sensor stream and SBP only in a 31-instance subset; van Rossum's scale max 11 vs 14 — corrected at verification, which found SBP present in Wilson and no maximum score stated there). P3 the score needs a declared aggregation rule — CONTESTED and consequential (alert rate 1.2–2/patient-day at 1 h vs 70 at 1 min). P4 unchanged thresholds are applied in service — NOT DOCUMENTED; one feasibility study deliberately ran continuous monitoring without alarms. P5 a paired cohort exists — ESTABLISHED (van Rossum n=46; Wilson n=41 of 48). P6 a published calibration exists to survive — FALSE (Gerry 2020: calibration assessed in 8/22 development models, 36%); and Gerry p12 verbatim, "Calibration of an integer scoring system cannot be assessed because it relies on the model producing predicted probabilities", so NEWS2 as published has no intercept or slope to transport at all.
What would count as an answer: Both streams scored on the same patients under the pre-declared rule, reporting the six estimands per stream; a within-intermittent-stream test of whether measurement intensity (time since last set, sets/24 h, clinician-initiated escalation) adds prognostic information beyond the values; the intercept/slope/threshold map restoring the intermittent operating point; and a declared bound on how much of the cross-stream gap is measurand mismatch rather than timing. Equal calibration and operating point answers in the negative and licenses reusing thresholds.
Novelty — queries run (query → one-line result): 29 distinct queries — 11 at Gate 2, 9 by adversary 1, 9 by adversary 2, all three logs with full lists in batches/2026-10-17-1619/UQ-20261017-39-record.md, -adversary-1.md and -adversary-2.md. Most informative: (1) "NEWS computed from continuous wearable monitoring ward alert rate positive predictive value" [mandatory own-field obvious-title query] → van Rossum 2023 JMIR Periop Med e44483, the candidate's alternative formulation #2 almost verbatim; (2) "early warning score validation bias vital signs recorded more frequently in deteriorating patients inflates discrimination" → Jarvis 2015, the candidate's own mechanism as a paper's stated motivation; (3) "informative observation times irregular visit process joint model dynamic prediction outcome-dependent sampling" [method-owning field] → active biostatistics literature (arXiv 2410.13113, 2602.15374); (4) adversary-2 "BMC Digital Health 2025 continuous wireless vital sign monitoring ward NEWS comparison intermittent nurse measurements" → opened the paper Gate 2 recorded as COULD NOT READ (Wilson 2025), a second paired-stream NEWS2 prior; adversary 1 opened the same paper on the publisher host on its first call; (5) adversary-2 ""clinical presence" shift prediction model calibration informative observation process" → Jeanselme et al. arXiv 2508.05472 (2025), the timing limb plus transport formalised and named in the method-owning field. Ledger duplicate check: INDEX.md read in full (the generated figure said 134 entries; the committed index at the time held 125, corrected at verification — the duplicate check itself was run against the real file); no duplicate (UQ-20261015-21, -20261016-16, -20261016-42 separated in the record).
Novelty — nearest prior formulations (3, with sources):
N1. van Rossum M et al., "Early Warning Scores to Support Continuous Wireless Vital Sign Monitoring for Complication Prediction in Patients on Surgical Wards", JMIR Perioper Med 2023;6:e44483 — periop.jmir.org/2023/1/e44483 (opened by Gate 2 and re-verified in full by adversary 2). Unit: aggregation window within 46 analysed surgical inpatients carrying per-minute sensor data and nurse sets ≥3/day. Endpoint: postoperative complication onset, alarms early (≤24 h) / late / false. Comparator: the same patients' nurse-measured EWS, and single-parameter alarms. Estimand: early sensitivity, alarms/patient-day, FDR vs threshold (1–9) and window (1–240 min). Threshold 3: 80%, 2 alarms/day, FDR 85%; threshold 5: 67%, 1.2/day; 70 alarms/day at 1-min windows; nurse EWS ≤40%.
N2. Wilson AJ et al., "The completeness, accuracy and impact on alerts, of wearable vital signs monitoring in hospitalised patients", BMC Digital Health 2025;3:13, doi 10.1186/s44247-025-00151-x (COSMIC-19) — recorded COULD NOT READ at Gate 2 (doi.org 429), opened independently by both adversaries. Unit: the paired score, 613 pairs in 41 of 48 inpatients. Streams: per-minute wearable vs concurrent 1–12-hourly nurse observations, same patients and hours. Score: partial NEWS2, published thresholds applied UNCHANGED (5+, 7+), aggregation = median of the preceding 5 min. Result: median wearable NEWS2 4 (IQR 3–6) vs nurse 1 (IQR 1–2); 86% (225/262) of 5+ and 89% (82/92) of 7+ wearable alerts false positive; conclusion that wearable data "should not be used in existing track and trigger systems", with re-developed thresholds as future work.
N3. Jarvis SW et al., "Are observation selection methods important when comparing early warning score performance?", Resuscitation 2015;90:1–6 — record opened at a Bournemouth repository record only; ScienceDirect not opened by either pass, so its numbers remain second-hand (flagged, not treated as a check that passed). Unit: the observation set, ~1.56M sets. Endpoint: death within 24 h. Comparator: three observation-selection schemes across 35 EWSs. Estimand: AUROC and score rank order. Finding: rank order invariant, AUROCs significantly higher under one-set-per-episode selection including for NEWS; stated motivation is the candidate's mechanism.
(Supporting, not graded: Agniel 2018 BMJ 361:k1479 — process out-predicts values in 118/174 lab tests; Gerry 2020 BMJ 369:m1501 — opened in full by adversary 2, quotations verified including the integer-score calibration sentence; Jeanselme 2025 arXiv 2508.05472 — "clinical presence shift", abstract only.)
Novelty — how this differs from each: vs N1 — N1 executes the candidate's own alternative formulation #2 on a paired cohort with the exact aggregation-window sweep the candidate claimed as novel; residual is calibration transport, a lead-time distribution, the recalibration map and the timing decomposition, none of which N1 reports. vs N2 — N2 does the same thing a second time on NEWS2 itself at unchanged published thresholds, and reaches the deployment conclusion the candidate called unowned; it reports no AUROC, no calibration, no alert rate per patient-day, no lead-time distribution, no recalibration, no timing test. vs N3 — same mechanism, same unit, but entirely within the intermittent stream: comparator is one selection scheme against another rather than one instrument against another, and the estimand is AUROC and ranking, not calibration or operating point. The residual conjunction is real and was found unpublished under 29 queries in nine vocabularies; it is an increment on two executed studies whose headline numbers already exist, and the candidate's framing that "the published operating point was never defined against the within-patient distribution" is false as stated.
Novelty confidence: Low
Significance — consequence: If unchanged thresholds transported, hospitals could pipe continuous streams into existing escalation rules. They do not, and the direction is already in print from two paired cohorts: the whole monitored population sits nearer the trigger, 83–89% of alerts are false, and the alert rate is set by the aggregation window (~35-fold from 1 h to 1 min) rather than by the patient. The timing limb would have the sharper consequence — if observation intensity carries information beyond the values, part of every published EWS AUROC is credit for the nurse's decision to measure and does not transfer to any automated stream.
Significance — audience: Digital-EWS configuration owners and deterioration committees choosing a window and a trigger; score custodians (RCP) who would have to state whether NEWS2 is defined on a continuous stream; continuous-monitoring vendors and their trials; prediction-model methodologists; HTA bodies. Real and identifiable, but (i)–(iii) can already act on N1 and N2, whose authors draw that conclusion themselves, and the audience for a calibration slope is thin where calibration is reported in 36% of development models and the score has no risk function.
Significance — fecundity: Whether every ward score has an aggregation-rule-dependent operating point and whether the dependence is monotone; whether observation timing belongs in deterioration models as an explicit covariate, and what happens when continuous monitoring removes a covariate the model was silently using; joint observation/outcome modelling transplanted into EWS development; whether continuous streams should be scored at all rather than modelled as trajectories; whether device NEWS2 needs its own respiratory-rate points.
Significance — anchoring: Alarm fatigue and false-alarm burden; the Gerry/Collins critique of EWS methodology; EHR process bias (Agniel 2018); informative-visit joint modelling and clinical presence shift (Jeanselme 2022, 2025); the ledger's performativity cluster (UQ-20261015-21). Sun et al. 2015 recalled only, unverified in all three passes.
Reason for silence: No credible mechanism survives. "New instrument" fails because the instrument arrived and the field asked the operating-point version immediately and twice (2023, 2025). "Disciplinary boundary" explains only why the two literatures do not read each other — it survives as a reason the specific conjunction of outcome tables was never written down (Gerry's 95-article review mentions continuous monitoring nowhere and does not treat clinician-chosen timing as a methodological issue; both paired papers report agreement and FDR and no calibration), but the method-owning field has formalised the general question under its own name. The record's third mechanism is self-defeating: the silence on the headline is best explained by the candidate's own false premise (measurand mismatch swamps the timing term), which per LEDGER.md makes the novelty finding suspect rather than marking a frontier.
